utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have spoken again to Judge Chowhan. He's plainly not well and, quite rightly, has decided that he shouldn't sit today. But we will continue on the same basis as before, anticipating that he will be back with us on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall sit in this session until 12.45. Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Welcome back. We were talking about the --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We were talking yesterday about the 9th of April, 1999, VJ collegium meeting. I want to ask you, in April and May and June of 1999 when you were part of the Supreme Command Staff, where -- where were you -- where were you housed? Where were you having your meetings and conducting your business? Were you always in the same location?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999, from the time I started coming there, the Supreme Command Staff was located at its place. As for specific meetings, which is what you address, or the one on the 9th of April, well, that meeting was held elsewhere in order to promote our chances of carrying out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us where you -- where your usual place was that the Supreme Command Staff was housed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff was in its building at its command post in an underground facility in Dreiser Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the 9th of April when you had this particular meeting, where was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was not held at the command post. It was held in a different room in an amphitheatre. It was a large conference hall of the military medical academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know where Mr. Milosevic, as the supreme commander, where was he generally working during April, May, and June of 1999, was it near where the Supreme Command Staff was located, was it in the same building?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was sometimes at the command post. Now, where he located for any reason, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did you attend any meetings at which Mr. Milosevic was present in April, May, and June 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. General, did you ever hear of a body called the Inter-departmental Staff for Combatting Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija? Did you ever hear of that group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't heard of that term until I was being prepped for this mission that I am now carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiarised with a different term, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the other term or the different term you were familiarised with?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that I made three lengthier visits to both the command post of the Pristina Corps -- the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, and the forward command post of the 3rd Army; likewise, I said that I spent some time at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, whereas some of the time I spent in the Pec barracks, where I attended meetings, as I had been ordered to do by the army commander. He told me to attend meetings by the MUP staff. The MUP staff had previously relocated to the Pec barracks military club. Later on, based on documents that were shown me yesterday and documents that were delivered to me, I realised that the commander used the term "to the overall commander of the MUP" in one of the documents, and in another document where he is issuing me orders to grant approval to General Pavkovic to attend meetings, he uses the term "Joint Command." It was then that I heard the term for the first time. In plain language I had also heard of the MUP operations staff. These are the terms that I came across at various points in time and terms that I gleaned from a variety of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were being prepped for this mission - as you termed it - you said you -- this was the first time you heard of this body called the Inter-departmental Staff for Combatting Terrorism. Were you shown any documents relating to that body in your preparation for testifying here?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had access to all documents that were submitted to the law office, through the National Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. Based on my practice and my work, I know that this is the gist of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But before your preparation for this testimony, you had not heard of that body. You weren't aware of its existence back in 1998 or 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying it's not correct, your comment, your question; it's partly correct. As I said before, when I was at the Pristina Corps forward command post he ordered me by phone to go to the Pec barracks and attend meetings of the MUP staff. Later on, he ordered me, following a request of the overall MUP commander, to issue an approval for the army units to be used. When I was at the forward command post of the 3rd Army, he ordered me to grant approval to General Pavkovic for him to go to meetings of the Joint Command. And that's when I heard it. As I was studying documents while preparing for this testimony, I eventually learned what you have just asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have confused you with my earlier question. The body I was talking about was one that apparently met in Belgrade. Were you aware of such a body that met in Belgrade in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that you confused me. I know that this body met in Belgrade, based on these documents that I'm looking at now. But back then I didn't know what this body was called. I just knew that these meetings were taking place at President Milosevic's. On behalf of the army, what I can say is that the Chief of the General Staff was there, the chief of the security administration, the commander of the 3rd Army, and the commander of the Pristina Corps, or rather, General Pavkovic, General Samardzic, General Perisic. If you're asking me about 1998, those persons were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are saying that the Inter-departmental Staff referred to by Mr. Hannis and the Joint Command were one and the same body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I answered when I heard about this term. As for this lower term, "Joint Command," I had heard this from a variety of sources back in 1998. I know where it was held, in Pristina or in 1998 in Pec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But when you were being asked about the Inter-departmental Staff, you answered that question by saying although you hadn't heard that name, you were aware of the Joint Command because you had been told to authorise General Pavkovic's attendance there. And what I wanted to be clear about is whether you think of them as the same body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Mr. Prosecutor asked me about the operations inter-departmental staff, and it was in that sense that I tried to provide an answer. This operations inter-departmental staff as far as I know, based on my study of any literature that I had access to following these events, this was the staff at President Milosevic's level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And you mention attending meetings of I think what you referred to as the MUP staff in Pec in 1998. Can you tell us how many meetings you attended and when those were?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already pointed out, these meetings were held in the conference hall of the Pec barracks military club. I attended three or four days because of certain disagreements, difference of opinion with certain senior officers of the MUP. I asked my commander that I not attend those meetings anymore and that I be sent back to Nis, which he accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you give us some approximate dates of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specify the dates. I said that I was there between the 29th and the 8th of June. If you take into account that I spent three or four days at the Pristina Corps forward command post, then you can deduct that from the total time I spent there and the remaining time is the time I spent in Pec. It has been a very long time, which leaves me unable to tell you the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's very helpful. Then that would have been during your first period in Kosovo in 1998 when you attended these meetings at the Pec barracks, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you the only representative of the VJ that attended those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you recall for us now who was there from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can name some persons, but I can't remember everybody's name. Vlastimir Djordjevic, a general; General Obrad Stevanovic; General Sreten Lukic; Mr. Frenki Simatovic I think; and Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there -- were you able to distinguish or was -- did anyone present themselves to you as being the MUP person in charge?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you talk about with them in these meetings in general, General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These meetings were used to discuss the current situation in Kosovo and Metohija, the focus being on the general Djakovica-Decani area. We discussed what measures the MUP people were taking, what the army people were doing in terms of securing the state border and the border belt, its own facilities and units included, what the MUP intended to do the next day, where and how the army should provide them with support in terms of their own deployment within the border belt or while securing the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And was there anybody else at this meeting other than yourself on behalf of the army and representatives of the MUP, including those you named for us earlier, were there any civilians or politicians present at this meeting -- or at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was just this one day that the army commander attended next to me. He came for a particular purpose because it was on that day that the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Sainovic, was supposed to arrive as well as Mr. Lilic. It was just that one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so General Samardzic came with you on that day because Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lilic were supposed to come to Kosovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but given the fact that they were about to arrive in Kosovo, the army commander, because this was his area of responsibility and there were high-ranking officials arriving, the federal deputy prime minister, the former president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, so he believed that his assessment, his contribution, would be more important in any which way than if, for example, his contribution was made by his own Chief of Staff and also in order to be a good host to these people. So that's why he did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lilic arrive or did you meet with them that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lilic arrived or landed at the heliport there, they came by helicopter. I welcomed them at the heliport and took them to a certain room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this -- was this in Pec?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Pec. That's what we're talking about, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you attend the meeting or whatever took place in the room to where you took them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I was present alongside with the commander. It was the commander who had arrived earlier on. He had heard me out, he heard my opinion, my assessment, sometimes he agreed, sometimes he disagreed, and he had the right to disagree. And he presented an assessment. It was him who presented the assessment, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So General Samardzic presented an assessment to Mr. Sainovic and General Lilic. Who else was present in the room during this presentation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the above-mentioned MUP officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what transpired after the presentation by General Samardzic, was it just an informational meeting for Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lilic or were any decisions taken?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We have to wait up for the interpretation. This was just about sharing information on the situation in Kosovo and Metohija; it was not a textbook briefing, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, I want to return now again to April 1999 and the VJ collegium meeting on the 9th. You told us that was held in an amphitheatre at the -- was that at the army medical centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this was -- this was a planning meeting or it turned into a planning meeting, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't categorically confirm this by saying yes. Planning normally follows conclusions and positions adopted. If the chief of the Supreme Command Staff had decided differently based on those briefings, if his conclusions had been different, maybe the directive would not have been drafted to begin with; however, in this case this took place on a regular basis in order to assess the entire complex situation that we were facing after 17 days of war and to see where to go next. Could we still keep the operative deployment that was carried out based on a previous plan? Or maybe certain amendments needed to be made by perhaps additional orders or by drafting a new directive altogether. In this particular case he opted to go for a new directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I understand that that meeting started out as an analysis of the situation up to that date regarding what had happened in the first 16 or 17 days of the conflict. But at the end of the meeting didn't General Ojdanic decide that you all on the Supreme Command Staff should sit down and write up some conclusions and make some recommendations that he would then present to the Supreme Command? That's what happened on the 9th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may have realised what all the participants talked about at that briefing. They analysed the situation, they presented problems, and they also made proposals, where, what, how, and when in terms of the country's defence. In addition to making proposals that a new document be drafted, we also proposed to the state leaders that measures be taken in order to deal with our problems. It was in that sense that he handed out an assignment to us, each in our own sector and department to further corroborate any information presented at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit P929 and at page 39 of the Serbian and page 34 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to show you a paragraph of what General Kovacevic had to say and ask you a question about that. And General Kovacevic was, as I understand, the assistant chief for operations and staff affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he gave a fairly detailed summary of the situation regarding what had happened during those first 16 or 17 days and what the situation was in terms of resources. Could you look at the last paragraph on that page you have before you. Could you read that out for us so I can be sure that the translation is correct, and then I'll have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, it's the last paragraph, right, and it reads: "And finally, I had skipped that, but there let me say it, I want to confirm everything that I have heard and everything that happens to be my own opinion. We must hold negotiations when we're on high ground. Over the 16 days of war so far we have achieved - and I must say this - enviable results. I will use that expression 'enviable results,' and we said, or rather, I said we can press on for another seven to ten days. This is the ideal time-frame for negotiations. When we start falling down, the odds we shall be facing will be steeper and steeper. We might end up facing a situation in which there will be nothing for us to negotiate for but we'll have no choice but to accept any terms foisted on us. "So much from me, General, sir."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Simic, would it be fair to say that there was some consensus within the Supreme Command Staff that that was the position, that you had done well up to that point, but things were only going to get worse and that the best option would be to try and negotiate some sort of settlement or some sort of peace. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, but I must add this. This conviction held by the Supreme Command Staff, starting with General Ojdanic and onwards, had existed much earlier on already, bearing in mind the situation in our army and the type of equipment that was available to us at the time and also bearing in mind the kind of military power that we would soon be up against. So that was everybody's conviction in the army, but the army is only an instrument of the politics; and I do not wish to further elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the end of the meeting, as we talked about yesterday, General Ojdanic said that he would take the results of your Supreme Command Staff's work and present it to the Supreme Command, perhaps the next day. And we talked a little bit about Supreme Command yesterday, but I want to ask you about someone else's description of the Supreme Command. You know General Milorad Obradovic, don't you, he was also a colleague of yours on the Supreme Command Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He testified earlier in this case and I want to read from the transcript at page 151 --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I have to apologise here. Are you referring to 1999, that he was a colleague of mine in the Supreme Command Staff? Milorad Obradovic in 1999, if I remember correctly, was the commander of the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did he take up that position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me read from the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The evidence is at the end of March 1999. He had until then been on the General Staff in charge of the operations and staff sector I think, and then he became commander of the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with that, General, does that sound about right, the end of March?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I can't confirm that. At the time when I arrived there on the 2nd or the 4th of April to assume my duty at the Supreme Command Staff, he was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read from the transcript at page 15128. Judge Bonomy is asking the question to General Obradovic, and the question is: "Are you familiar with the expression 'Supreme Command'?" General Obradovic's answer is: "That term was used when the state of war was proclaimed. There was the president of the republic, he commanded the army in war and peace, and then it went without saying that the Supreme Defence Council, as the Supreme Command -- well, this member of the Supreme Defence Council who was the head of state was the Commander-in-Chief, but basically the Commander-in-Chief was the Supreme Command, the Supreme Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY THEN SAID
utterances.text: "Obviously you're familiar then with the expression. If the Supreme Defence Council was effectively the same body if war and peace, can you explain why it had a different name in wartime?" General Obradovic then said: "The Supreme Defence Council functioned in war and peace. In peacetime it was called the Supreme Defence Council and once a state of war was declared it grew into the Supreme Command. That's what it was called. Otherwise, it is the Supreme Defence Council that practically commanded and decided on how the army was to be used in accordance with the constitution and law." Now, would you disagree with General Obradovic that during the state of war the Supreme Defence Council became the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree 50 per cent with the statement made by General Obradovic, and I explained yesterday why that was so. Principally that was because of the principle of singleness of command in the decision-making process. If you allow me, Mr. Prosecutor, if this had been the case that the Supreme Council becomes part of the Supreme Command, the Supreme Defence Council, if it were to become the Supreme Command and the Commander-in-Chief comes out of the Supreme Command, would that mean that the supreme commander or the Commander-in-Chief was the commander commanding over the other two members of the Supreme Defence Council? That was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So which 50 per cent of that do you agree with then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the part of the statement where he said that the president in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council commands the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, as a result of that meeting on April 9th, the Supreme Command Staff created a directive, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think we may have looked at that the other day or you may have seen that, that's Exhibit P1481.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could have that up on the screen. I would like to go to page 5 of both the English and the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While that's being organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just follow-up briefly on what you've been asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did the Supreme Defence Council meet after the war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot give you an answer to your question because I don't know. It appears to me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're about to say something. It appears to you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that in 1998 in December, it met for the last time in its full composition, and in October it would meet again in its full composition and a decision was made that if the country should come under an attack it would defend itself using all its forces, all its assets. That's what I know. I can't tell you anything more specific about 1999 because I didn't see anything about that in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, on page 5 of the directive of April 9th there was in -- I guess it's about the middle of the page there you see there's a reference to the 2nd Stage, Phase 1 and Phase 2. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it says: "On certain axes of the state border, organise reception of refugees ..." Now, can you tell me what "certain axes of the state border" meant? Was that limited to certain locations or certain borders? Can you explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, this was a reference to the official interstate border crossings where it was possible to record the exit and return of the refugees in order to be able to verify possible presence of any terrorists in their ranks. Any crossings outside of the official border crossings are considered illegal crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would those -- do you know, would those refugees have been allowed to return if they did not have the necessary identification documents showing that they had been previously citizens or residents of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. This was not in the military jurisdiction. The border crossings were under the jurisdiction of the MUP, so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under Phase 2 of the 2nd Stage it says: "Use persistent defence from the state frontier to prevent rapid breakthrough, create conditions to complete mobilisation, regroup and bring in forces to smash and eject the aggressor from the territory of the FRY." Now, was Phase 2 intended to happen after Phase 1, is that why they're listed in that order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aggression need not have been carried out in accordance with this scenario in the stages that we anticipated. The aggressor could have launched all its assets, ground forces, air force. If that had been the case, Phase 2 would have been activated immediately, full mobilisation, bringing in of all the forces, and fighting them. But we thought, based on our assessments, our experience, that they would follow this pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But Phase 1, which talks about organising reception of refugees also says that: "In the event the STS," and I understand that stands for Siptar terrorist forces, in the event they "infiltrate under the guise of returning refugees, prevent their infiltration." As a practical matter, the best way to infiltrate that is not to allow anybody to come back; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been saying for two days now that the objectives and the policies of the Army of Yugoslavia were not to expel our own population, people who lived for ages in this territory. Our objective was to destroy the terrorist army of Kosovo, whose goal was to achieve its political intentions by war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. It just seems to me that as a practical matter when you are in the midst of this aggression by NATO against your country and you've already spent the first two weeks trying to crush the KLA and drive them out, it doesn't make any sense to be opening the borders and letting refugees and possibly infiltrated terrorists back in. That just wasn't going to happen, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely what we feared the most. You cannot open your border, you cannot open it, and then have the people come to every ridge, every ravine, because you cannot effect any kind of control. But if you have a certain number of loyal citizens and thousands of terrorists coming back infiltrated into their ranks, then this brings your own forces in an inferior position in relation to the aggressor because now they have the superiority in terms of the forces that they intend to deploy in Kosovo and also the forces coming in from Albania. And it would be much more difficult to defend the country. So our goal was to prevent precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it seems to make sense to me that given the nature of the conflict in Kosovo leading up to the NATO aggression where you had KLA who would, I think using a term of one of our earlier witnesses, gun-and-run, they might be wearing their uniforms when they started shooting at the MUP and the VJ, but oftentimes they would take off their uniforms, put on civilian clothes, and mix in with the civilian population. And there was no way for the army or the police to tell a loyal Kosovo Albanian citizen from an infiltrated, now-wearing-civilian-clothes KLA fighter. That was the problem, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that was one problem. But even if they're identified because of the presence of the civilian population, the infirm, the children, the women, you saw from what I said yesterday that the Pristina Corps commander had risked his own troops in order to protect the population, lest there should be any civilian casualties. What would we have done in a situation where you have thousands of people dressed in civilian clothes and then you open fire; could anyone have dealt with this problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I suggest to you, General, that that was -- that was part of the reason why hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians, civilians and probably a fair number of KLA fighters, were removed, were directed out of Kosovo by the MUP and by the army in the first two weeks or so of the war after 24 March, because it was -- there was no way to separate them and tell which ones are which. It's just easier to send them all out, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, tell me how so. How is it not easier to do that than to try to tell whether this one's loyal and that one's a KLA fighter when you're being bombed by NATO at the same time. Isn't it just easier - my word is "easier" - isn't it just easier to get them out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You're entirely wrong. You view this problem in a completely wrong light. I don't want to any more severe words because this is not my place to do so. Let me tell you once again, the objective of my country, of the army where I served, where I was trained, where I served for 40 years was not to expel a single citizen out of their country, their homes. Our objective was to destroy the terrorist army of Kosovo which used illegal terrorist means to achieve their political goals. If I were to accept what you said, would that not be in contradiction with everything that I said over the past two days, corroborating that with the documents that indicate that commanders risked their own troops in order to protect the civilians, the Albanians. If you allow me to say a few more words. In the highest document, the directive of the Supreme Command Staff, does it not indicate in paragraph 2 a concept and idea of operation - we see it now in front of us, you perhaps on purpose decided not to ask me anything about that, and that's your right. But let me just read it. It says here: "To engage and use the Army of Yugoslavia in the defence against the NATO forces through all -- through those two stages with the full application of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and the international law and -- law of war and humanitarian law." General Ojdanic insisted on this in order to protect the entire population, that all tasks must be carried out abiding by the spirit that is presented here in this directive, in this part of the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was going to ask you about that, General. And you would agree with me that it's part of the Geneva Convention that no civilians should be forcibly transferred within their country or deported outside the state borders, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would agree with you that it's very nice that that provision is in this directive, but this directive is dated the 9th of April, 1999. By that time, hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians had already been deported, so this doesn't do them much good, does it, on the 9th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday when asked questions by the Judges and by the lawyers, I said that it was quite natural in all the wars all over the world for the civilian population to flee the areas where combat operations are carried out in order to protect their own lives, and it is only natural that it happened here too. We had an additional element here and that is the pressure on the part of the terrorist army of Kosovo, because they wanted to achieve this goal, as I explained yesterday in detail. I don't want to waste any more time here going through that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's an answer to my question, but I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that directive I'd like to turn now to page 11 of both the English and the B/C/S, and this is a section -- section 6 is entitled or translated as: "Command and communications."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on April the 9th it is talking about deployment of the Supreme Defence Council and the VJ General Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it says: "KM in current sectors," I think KM here means "command post" in current sectors, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where the command post for the Supreme Defence Council was, was it co-located with the General Staff at that time or did it have a separate location?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council at that time, I saw not only President Milosevic but also President Milutinovic at that site once. I didn't see Mr. Djukanovic, the president of Montenegro, there; and I assume -- but I don't actually assume, but I know that because it says it here that it was also the command post of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say you saw Milosevic and Milutinovic at that site once. Can you tell us where that site was and when you saw them there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the command post of the Supreme Command Staff was in an underground facility in Dreiserova Street in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's where you saw Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Milutinovic one time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it was after you had become a member of the Supreme Command Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely because had I not become a member of the Supreme Command Staff I would not have been able to get into that facility at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then it would have been before the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say before the end of the conflict; I would say during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. Now, let me go back to one thing regarding this directive. You had mentioned that directives -- I guess this was at page 15487, Mr. Visnjic asked you about what a directive was in the hierarchy of military documents. Your answer was: "Only the Supreme Command Staff can issue directives. It's the highest type of order." Now, weren't there directives issued in the VJ during peacetime before there was a Supreme Command Staff in place? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command issues directives when it wants to use the forces in a certain area. If you were referring to this directive and if you were alluding to the Grom 98 directive when the state of war was not declared, then my answer is yes. A directive is issued when the forces are to be used on a larger or smaller scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There may have been some confusion in prior questions, and your answer here you said: "The Supreme Command issues directives ..." I assume based on your previous answers you mean the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please try and understand what I'm saying. I'm trying to speak really clearly. When I say "the Supreme Command," I mean the commander and his staff. The supreme commander cannot sit down on his own and do everything that needed to be done with the documents technically, to distribute it to all the addressees; his staff have to do that. And that is why when I say "the Supreme Command," I'm not referring just to the supreme commander but his entire staff, Stab.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But would it also be fair to say that during peacetime before the imposition or declaration of a state of war, that the General Staff of the army could and did issue directives, like Grom 98?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's the difference between a directive and an order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there is a huge difference between a directive and an order issued to the commands of subordinate units. A directive is issued seldom, more seldom. It defines the concept for the use of forces over a longer period of time, perhaps a month, two, three days, until the end of the war. It all depends on the actual assessment of the situation, whether the developments are such that some corrections must be made to this directive. Orders at a lower level are in force for a shorter period of time, and they pertain to smaller-scale operations at tactical and operational level, and they are issued more often. So that would be the difference between a directive and an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we've in this trial had some discussion about a directive that was issued by General Perisic in the summer of 1998, and we've had at least one witness describe this as a -- what I would call a contingency plan. It was something that was a plan with specific details about how certain units would be deployed and what actions they should take if some triggering event happened; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Army of Yugoslavia there were no reserve plans or contingency plans. Yesterday I said that there are so-called initial operational plans that are made in peacetime on the basis of certain assessments and the expected modes of -- or security threats. As time goes by and as certain indicators of those threats are monitored, those initial operational plans are modified, amended, or, alternatively, new plans are made. There was no contingency plan at all, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we may just have a semantic problem here, General, because your description about: "As time goes by and as certain indicators of those threats are monitored, those initial operational plans are modified, amended, or, alternatively, new plans are made," to me that's what I would call a contingency plan. This is what I'm going to do if something happens; if that thing doesn't happen, then I may do something else. And I will wait and see what occurs between now and then. With my explanation of what I call a contingency plan, aren't we talking about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view and in essence, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll accept that. Let me move on to something else. Let me go --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, before I leave 929, if we still have that document, I'd like to go to page 12 of the B/C/S and of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just need to ask you a couple of terms. It's the -- I think it's the second line under the heading there, General, it says: "With KM -- with command post at M + 10 hours most important communications, at M + 20 hours for D, delta, all communications at full volume." Can you tell me what M and D, delta, stand for in that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This directive was issued straight away and came into force straight away. So here the Chief of Staff ordered that communications at M hours, M hours, that is to say, after 10.00, that communications should work; and D is the present day, today. D means day, "dan," meaning this day, today, and "cas" means the hour when the directive was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, General, I want to go to another topic now. You told us how you were part of a team assigned to inspect the Pristina Corps in late May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'd like to look now at Exhibit D -- 3D692.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after your team had conducted the inspection, I think you told us that General Velickovic wrote a report to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff about the results of your team's inspection of the Pristina Corps. And that's what that document is on the screen in front of you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I see in the original it says the inspection was carried out between 23 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Visnjic standing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's just disappeared, line 10, page 25, Mr. Hannis said that he will not be dealing with P929 any longer, or rather, I think that that is not what was shown to the witness. So I would like to have that corrected, please. It was P1481.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So all the references to 929 are --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, I had been talking about 929, which is the meeting of the VJ collegium, but the directive, when I was talking about the directive, that is P1481.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the directive arose from the VJ collegium meeting, and that's part of the basis for my confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, 3D692, I think there's a typo in that because it says the inspection was carried out between 23 and 16 May, that doesn't seem possible. Between the 23rd and the 26th of May, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen on the basis of the actual document, that it was registered on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. Now, you told us, I think, that you took part in two other inspections, one I think where you were inspected and another one where you were the team leader; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to say -- well, I do apologise to you. It is correct in part. I was no inspector. I was no inspection team. I've been explaining for the past two days that the Army of Yugoslavia has a separate organ that has far greater authorities. It is called the inspectorate of the Army of Yugoslavia. General Samardzic headed it during the course of the war, whereas these are checks that are carried out through the authority exercised by General Ojdanic. In this way he sees how the tasks that he set are being implemented. The inspection is not subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I see yesterday or the day before when you testified that this was translated as a control that you carried out. If I use that term, is that more correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. Assistance and control or check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm now confused. I thought control had been used in the context of inspection, but you're saying, no, control is a proper way to describe the report of the -- the visit between the 23rd and 26th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for having to explain this yet again. There are two organs in the Supreme Command Staff, one is a permanent organ, a standing organ, that is established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's enough if you just answer my question. Are you saying that "control" is a proper word to use to describe the visit between the 23rd and the 26th of May, because I understand that that's not an inspection by the inspectorate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if our English document is translated as "inspection," your position is that that -- that a different word should be used?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about this document, I claim to you that this is "control," and that is the only way in which this term can be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You understand, General, I only read the English, I don't read the Serbian and I'm going on what I read in front of me. So we'll call it "control" and this control that you carried out, you told us that you were involved in two others, one --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see two people standing up now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to deal with any further misunderstanding that may come up, perhaps it would be proper if the witness would read the heading and then the interpreters can interpret what he read out from the booth, and that way we're going to deal with this and have it clarified once and for all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Presiding Judge allow me to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Tour and exercising insight in the implementation of the tasks of the Pristina Corps report."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There you go, Mr. Hannis, you've almost got a full hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure we met the goal that Mr. Visnjic envisioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless I'm confused, this is the same document we had this discussion on yesterday, and Mr. Zecevic pointed out to us that that first paragraph doesn't deal with inspection, it deals with a tour. I thought that was cleared up yesterday. It may have been a different document, but I think it's the same document. And if he -- if you want to, you know, he could read the entire first paragraph and clarify that, but I'm told that that talks about a tour and not an inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I doubt if Mr. Hannis is too troubled about exactly what we call it, are you, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, not really, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not sure the same word -- well, I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- my recollection is the discussion about tour was about a different document from this one, but that's not to say that the two aren't similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I thought that was about General Perisic's expedition or whatever we call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'll use the term "control" or "tour" for this activity you were involved in, but I think you told us in your testimony that you also were involved in similar activities on two other occasions, one where you were the team leader and one where you were the person who was being looked at; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 50/50 is the correctness level. Once I said that I led a team and once I headed a team when a brigade was toured. Now, leading a team means having underneath you five or six other leaders controlling five or six other brigades. In this specific case it was General Velickovic, the control that you're asking me about right now. That is to say that I was never controlled, but you used the word "controlled," or at least that's the interpretation that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. But one time you were a team leader, which I take it to mean you did the same thing that General Velickovic did on this occasion; is that correct or am I only batting 50/50 still?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense you're saying 50/50, but let us clarify this as well. 26 people were there, out of them nine generals as heads of teams, so 30 per cent were generals. He alone with me commanded the corps command; the other generals with four or five colonels controlled one, a second, a third, or a fourth brigade. And then his responsibility was at highest level in terms of the reports from the controlled brigades, to summarize them and then explain them to the order issuing authority and propose measures if that is necessary. That is the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the core of the question I'm trying to ask you, I'm trying to find out about the occasion where you headed a team. Can you tell us when that was and where that was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 37th Brigade, the 37th Motorised Brigade, the broader region of Drenica, more narrower is Srbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And approximately when was that done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly whether it was in April from the 12th until the 14th or whether it was from the 12th to the 14th of May. I cannot say for sure. One of those two time-periods.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you write a report about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always. That's an elementary part of an order, General Ojdanic's order, that once the insight is carried out, once one refers to the command post and after the oral briefing that all of this is written up and handed over to him so that it would become a document of lasting value that is preserved in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 37th Brigade at that time, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time. I cannot recall each and every detail. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all right. Let me then go to this control report, 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one question before you do. And I don't need a detailed explanation for this. Was that tour of a different nature from the one referred to in the exhibits on the screen? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just at lower level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could go to page 2 of the English and the B/C/S of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your -- the team that you were a part of on this occasion, General, did find out or did discover some shortcomings which you advised the commander of and wrote up in your report. I want to look at item number 1 under "Shortcomings noticed," and I'll read part of it and ask you a question. You found: "Daily and periodical analysis, briefings, task setting on brigade level and lower are missing from the daily command structure. Therefore, the commands are not familiar enough with the situation in the units, which provides favourable grounds for possible surprises." And then you say: "The 7th Infantry Brigade is a drastic example ..." To what extent was this a problem in the Pristina Corps? Did you find this to be a problem throughout all the brigades, 50 per cent, some number in between, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've read out is correct, but I cannot express myself in percentage terms, whether it was 50 or more, at any rate in a smaller number of units. And you see here it says the 7th Infantry Brigade, that was a brigade that was mobilised 100 per cent. That is why it was more difficult there to establish order, military discipline, and so on. That is why I'm saying that in part of the units there were such weaknesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've heard some other evidence earlier in this trial that the 7th Brigade in late May, I think the 18th or 19th, had deserted almost en masse, is that correct, the whole brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not fully correct. One or two battalions deserted as far as I can remember, not the entire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many men would that be approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are bringing me into a situation where I have to express myself in percentage terms, and that would be 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 40 per cent of the entire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what would be the full strength of a brigade, how many men would that be?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one battalion -- well, it depends. Don't take my word for each and every number. I cannot say. Motorised or infantry battalion has between 500 and 700 men, whereas a brigade has between three to five such battalions. Again, it depends on the type of brigade, there are infantry brigades, motorised brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get a rough figure whether we're talking about a hundred or a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Later on in that paragraph you say: "So the fact that the command staff was astonished by the desertion of about 2.000 men within two days, 18 to 19 May, is not surprising." So that 2.000 number, that's not just the 7th Brigade but that's other Pristina Corps deserters as well? That's the total number for the entire Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you take this, it is a summary report of the leader of the team that was conducting the tour; that is what I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to ask you now about paragraph 4. It says: "There's a lack of discipline in a part of the units as regards personal appearance, behaviour, and the application of instructions regulating certain combat activities." Can you explain for us what kind of instructions regarding combat activities that there was a lack of discipline in connection with their application?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, in addition to the peacetime composition, the Pristina Corps had part of its reserve units, too, that, due to the brevity of time and the fact that the aggression had begun, and also you heard in my remarks, or rather, you saw what I said at the collegium on the 9th of April when I claimed that it -- that we were not supposed to expect an aggression in 10 or 15 days, which is favourable for us so that we can do away with the noted weaknesses and that we are ready when a possible land aggression takes place. This is exactly what it refers to here. There was a lack of discipline on the part of reservists and some volunteers, there were desertions from positions, they were leaving positions arbitrarily. In the 37th unit, for example, they were playing a game and they suffered an air-strike. And I don't know exactly -- please don't take my word for -- as far as the number is concerned, but there were seven to ten casualties. That means that the position was not protected enough from air-strikes. There was not enough surveillance of the facilities in terms of providing security for the unit as a whole. This is the kind of lack of discipline that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did your -- did this team that you were a part of with regard to lack of discipline and as regards behaviour and application of instructions, did you find any instances by the reserves or by actual VJ professional soldiers any instances of looting or of burning houses or mistreatment of civilians? Any instances of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we mentioned in the context of these witnesses is what we saw through our own insight and in the reports of generals who headed the mentioned units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you've answered my question. Did you become aware of any instances of looting or arson or mistreatment of civilians by VJ or VJ reserve?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know in those two days while we were there, we did not notice such things, but on the basis of combat reports I did have knowledge to the effect that there were such occurrences, individual cases of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's not unusual, is it? I mean, an army during wartime, you have thousands of men out in the field in stressful conditions, that happens in all armies of the world, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you admitted to what I was telling you about the population fleeing from endangered areas. No matter how hard you try to have this conducted in an orderly fashion, it is not always possible. Even in peacetime a state organises certain things, but then there are individual cases of the opposite taking place. But it's not the system that regulates it to be that way. The system, on the contrary, fought against such phenomena that are not in line with soldierly conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it that you then agree with me. Let me ask you about number 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do. I'm struggling to understand what you say there, Mr. Simic, about now Mr. Hannis has admitted to what I was telling you about the population fleeing from endangered areas. Could you explain that more fully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman, the Prosecutor, put a leading question when he said: Is it not something that usually happens, that it's not unusual, that in any army during war there is looting, lack of discipline, and so on. My answer was that in an indirect way he went back to the answer that I had given in relation to the fact that the population was fleeing from zones of combat activity for the sake of their personal safety and security, which is also usual in all wars throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I still don't understand. My immediate reaction was that you were suggesting that the conduct of soldiers was driving the population from endangered areas, but that's not what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It just seemed an odd link for you to make. But please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 7, still on the same document, says: "A large number of reserve officers are untrained for certain functional tasks. With certain reserve officers there's also the question of intellectual ability as regards responsibility for commanding men in an armed conflict." So the team you were a part of found that there were certain reserve officers who were not intellectually up to the job of commanding men in war, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have to scroll up just a little bit for you to see number 7. Sorry about that, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is correct, right, you found that there was a large number of reserve officers who didn't have the intellectual capability for the job?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to give you a short answer, it would be yes, but if you allow me to explain I can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'll allow you to explain if you'll keep it very short.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be short because of the interpretation, but otherwise I could keep my explanation down to a minute were it not for that. One must bear in mind the fact that the reserve officers' school is normally completed by secondary-school-age young men or university-educated young men at an ideal age, and then they dedicate themselves to their civilian callings. It is usual for us to take a three- to five-year period, and then we use one-month conditionings in the Army of Yugoslavia based on their functions. Since 1990 we were in a very difficult situation financially and it had been a long time since they were trained and schooled, there had been changes to their physical and mental set-up, and we were not able to use conditioning to bring their ability up to the desired level. The war was foisted on us and we ran out of time, the 10 to 15 days necessary to train these men or their units. And the decision is a result of what I have just established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that problem of a large number of men without that ability creates problems with discipline of the combat troops, the men under their supervision, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. If you have a leader who is not skilled or able, the result you normally obtain is not the desired one, often quite the opposite, in fact. But we did deal with that problem later on, and if you look at the proposals made to the Supreme Command Staff, that soon becomes clear. Just use this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But this is late May, so up until May this has been a problem, correct, in the Pristina Corps? Just yes or no if you can.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not yes or no, part yes and part no. It wasn't a general problem, it was a partial problem in some units that had been fully mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me turn to page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see paragraph 11, General, I want to read part of that. One of the shortcomings you noted was: "There is no single command over all the forces in the zone of responsibility. All contacts with the units of the MUP are established by agreement, which is often disobeyed, especially at the lower levels. "Despite the fact that this cooperation is functioning for now, in more difficult situations of crisis and when there is not enough time available, this could have serious consequences both for members of the VJ and the MUP." Let me stop there. When you noted this problem you said, "This cooperation is functioning for now." Did you find any evidence to suggest that during the first -- the first two or three weeks of the war that there had been a problem of cooperation between the MUP and the VJ that caused any military disasters or failures to carry out combat task?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've just read out is entirely correct. We bore in mind the order of the supreme commander President Milosevic, dated the 18th of April on the resubordination of the MUP. It was along these lines that we underlined this particular remark, that this never came to those levels. It was observed at lower levels that brigade commanders, regiment commanders, and commanders of certain lower-ranked MUP units facing the same kind of problem in the field coordinated among themselves, and then we had situations in certain units where they accepted this and resubordinated themselves to a particular army commander only in relation of that particular part of the implementation of a combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Before that order was issued we have evidence that in the first two and three weeks of the war there were joint operations between the MUP and the VJ. Are you aware of that? That before the subordination order was issued on the 18th of April, there had been joint operations between the MUP and the VJ, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't at the Supreme Command Staff at the time. I can't comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you were at the Supreme Command on the 3rd or 4th of April, right, and the order was issued on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about between those dates, hadn't there been joint operations between the MUP and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the spirit of certain orders by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read on. "There had been reactions at all levels to the 'privileged' position of members of the MUP in relation to members of the VJ" regarding "regular payment of daily allowances and salaries, supply of uniforms, communications equipment, replacement every two months, et cetera)." That was a problem for the army, wasn't it, that the average line soldier felt that the average policeman was getting better treatment, better pay, better equipment? That was the situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next paragraph says that: "Members of the VJ are particularly irritated by the behaviour of special police units who are in the brigades' zone of responsibility (lack of respect for agreements and looting)." So you became aware that there were allegations that the special police units were engaged in looting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would receive this earlier on as well, certain reports telling us about unseemly behaviour on the part of certain members of the MUP, the focus being on the fact that they were not observing agreements reached at those evening meetings about carrying out combat operations. If you allow - and I think we saw that yesterday - as far as I remember, the Pristina Corps commander, or rather, the army commander, too, at the time ordered and set up his own patrols and MUP patrols, the objective being that whatever was looted by either side would be seized, recorded, sent back to the 202nd logistics base. They would then take statements from any perpetrators and send these stolen goods back to those that they had been taken from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what the logistics base would have done in the situation where the owners of the stolen goods were no longer living in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we go on there's a translation error that should get picked up otherwise we're going to miss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Line 14 of the previous page, 41, the witness in Serbian said "pojedinci MUP," which I believe translates into individual members of the MUP not members of the MUP as a general category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Should I repeat my question, General, or do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for you to repeat. It is stated clearly and I stand by what I said because I was one of the people involved in producing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm not sure I understand what happens to the recovered stolen property that belonged to people, for example, Kosovo Albanians who are now in Albania or Macedonia, did the army then convert that property to its use?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you what the 202nd logistics base eventually did with those goods that were recorded and listed. I know that some goods, especially vehicles, were inspected, technicians inspected them in cases where repairs were needed, repairs were made, and the vehicles were placed at the disposal of whoever was most in need of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we have to break again at this stage for an hour. We'll resume at 1.45. Could you again please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I just want to follow-up on your control of the Pristina Corps with General Velickovic. You told us yesterday that when you returned you and he went and reported -- well, before you left you reported to the corps commander of the Pristina Corps. And then when you returned to Belgrade you reported to General Ojdanic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was just an oral report. Was he the only one besides you and General Velickovic who were involved in that report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I explained yesterday that -- I apologise. There were the evening oral briefings after our arrival at the command post. In addition to General Velickovic, I attended too in my capacity as his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But back at Belgrade did you report to the entire Supreme Command Staff or did you just report to General Ojdanic when you gave your oral report before you prepared your written report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following oral briefings the next day and based on the date on which a document was entered into the files, you can see that many dates elapsed. This was the 29th and we technically processed whatever we found at the object of our control and we wrote this in writing. This report is something that each member of the Supreme Command Staff had access to. There were certain weaknesses under the competence of members of the Supreme Command Staff, and these weaknesses had a bearing on each and every one of its members and these precisely were their tasks. So my answer is each member of the Supreme Command Staff was informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a reference to Velickovic being your deputy; is that accurate -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A reference to you being his deputy; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand the point you make about the other members of the Supreme Command Staff needing to be able to see the results of this control as it might affect areas under their competency. But what I was driving at, what I was trying to find out, General, was: As I understand it you and General Velickovic upon your return to Belgrade gave an oral briefing to General Ojdanic about what you had found. And you did that, I take it, before you wrote up your final report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it just the three of you in that meeting when you gave General Ojdanic the briefing or was that done in front of the whole Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic and the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that meeting did General Ojdanic give you any direction about what you should or should not include in your written report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary. He accepted everything. The only task he gave us was: Do this as soon as possible so that one could go to the 3rd Army command in order to deal with the tasks. He entirely accepted the situation that we found and the problems that we noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- General Velickovic is a new name to me I think, although I can't claim to know all the -- or remember all the names involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He was named in the document about the control as being the team leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And our General Simic here was the deputy team leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And remind me of the date of the control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 23rd to the 26th of May, and his name is the one who appears on the report which is 3D692.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was General Velickovic's normal responsibility, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean in terms of his functional responsibility, the late General Velickovic was assistant chief of the staff of the Supreme Command for the air force and anti-aircraft defence.
