Therefore, he was one of the assistants for some aspects of the country's defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I want to move on to some of the areas that Mr. Ackerman, the lawyer for General Pavkovic, covered with you yesterday. One of the first thing he asked you about was when the clashes between the 3rd Army, Pristina Corps, and the KLA began or first started happening and your answer was: "May, later May, June, July, that's when this became particularly prominent and this was going on in the border belt." During May, June, and July 1998, weren't there also clashes between the KLA and the army in areas outside the border belt or in the interior of Kosovo? It wasn't just limited to the border belt, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If memory serves me, I stated yesterday that within the border belt and in terms of securing the border belt and opening fire, no order was required, no special order was required. This was regulated by the rules of service applying to the border area, and this is all the authority that the units securing the border need. I also said that certain places where operations were carried out were outside the border belt, but near those roads, such as Smonica and the supply route to our units at the border posts were cut and that is why clashes erupted on the one hand. On the other, our units in the area were often being attacked; as a response, clashes would break out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And some of those clashes in the summer of 1998 were in the interior Kosovo and some of those, indeed, were not on the roads; isn't that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be, it may not be. Yes it is correct if your interpretation is that this is the interior of Kosovo because it's quite far from the border belt, but if you take into account the fact that this was near the roads and that this posed a threat to supply routes, then, yes, you might say that clashes broke out in the more central areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ackerman asked you about whether the VJ had full authority to respond to an attack at any time, and you said that the VJ rules of service provided unambiguously, unequivocally that any unit under attack must use any means available to protect itself, and I understand that. But I take it when you say there "under attack," that means right at the moment. Your VJ unit is out there and it is being fired upon. That's what you mean when you say "under attack," correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me an attack is any form where weapons of any kind are being used. You use the term "firing" this could also be interpreted as artillery firing. Therefore I would be more in favour of saying this: An attack during which weapons are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I don't understand that to mean if, for example, the VJ had been attacked while travelling down the road between Pristina and Pec on Tuesday, I don't take your answer to mean that a week later the VJ can go to a village near the point on the road where they were attacked and attempt to clean it out of any suspected terrorist that might have been involved in the shooting the week before? That's not a response to the attack, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably if your information is correct, this was support lent to the MUP units involved in the operation, the operation aimed at liquidating the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right. It would be the MUP's job to deal with these terrorists that might have been involved in an attack on the VJ a week earlier, we agree about that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the focal point for these operations, that's right, but the army was lending a certain degree of support by its presence and in terms of its equipment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And included in the equipment that the VJ was employing to support the MUP in some of these anti-terrorist operations in the summer of 1998, sometimes that included heavy weapons like artillery pieces, tanks, et cetera, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, you mentioned to Mr. Ackerman about some weapons depots or ammunition depots where the materials were moved in -- or relocated in 1998 and you mention -- it's spelled Bair, I don't know how to pronounce that, and Lukare. Do I have those names right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I served 15 years in Pristina, so I went all over Kosovo. Bair and Lukare, that's what these two places were called. That's where we had our depots for wartime materiel reserves, or rather, weapons of all calibres. That order stipulated that because the situation was getting more complex and was, indeed, deteriorating and because of the context. Is that enough? Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to verify the locations. Can you tell me where Bair was located, I can't find it on my map of Kosovo and maybe it's because I don't have the right spelling. Do you recall where it was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's, as far as I can recall, between Mitrovica further south in the direction of Obilic. Perhaps you can't find it on this map because it's a small place and this is a small-scale map, perhaps. And Lukare is to the north-east on the Pristina-Leskovac road near Kacikol, 5 or 6 kilometres away from Pristina, to the north-east. You should have it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could pull up Exhibit P615. I think it's page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did find a Lukare just north of Pristina, and I wanted to ask you, General, if that's the right one?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Lukare, not straight north, but more to the north-east, but yes, I would agree with you if you said to the north, that's Lukare. It's on the Pristina-Kacikol-Leskovac road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can zoom in on the quadrant showing Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, can you see that, can you see Lukare there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to the north-east, you can see it, Lukare, it's written there. Sinji Dol, and there to the east of that, it says Lukare.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By the scale of that map it appears to be -- it's about maybe 2 kilometres away from Pristina. You told us yesterday that this was an area that was 100 per cent Albanian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Majority Albanian population, but in the closer area around it that's 100 per cent, I think you could say that, but it's not merely because the Albanians lived there but for other reasons, too, because of this road and of the way -- because of the way in which the Siptars built their villages, the streets are narrow, you have high, thick walls, 2 or more metres high, and it is impossible for two vehicles to bypass each other the streets are so narrow. And that is why we thought that if the situation got any more complex we would be unable to relocate, to remove those huge amounts of weaponry that was there in case of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I only ask because you indicate those two areas were 100 per cent Albanian populated. I want to go now to the time when you were chief of --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have -- that may have been a slip of the tongue, but I gave you the right reason, the proper reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You were Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army. When did you start in that position? We know when you ended, but when did you begin?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I took over on the 7th of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I must have missed that. And you mentioned that you were deputy commander. Was it deputy commander for the same period of time or did you hold both those positions at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I stated. Perhaps that was the translation you received or whatever, but I stated that I had taken over the post of the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army on the 7th of July, 1996, in Nis. And in accordance with the establishment, that post means that I am the deputy commander of the 3rd Army. It does not mean that I discharged both duties at the same time, although this is not out of the question, you cannot rule that out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: We didn't hear the last part of the witness's answer because the counsel's microphone was not switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need to explain that again. It doesn't -- it's difficult for me to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the command of the 3rd Army has its commander; at that time it was General Dusan Samardzic. And I was the chief of operations administration at the General Staff, and by a decree of the president of the state I was appointed the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army and at the same time I was the deputy commander of the 3rd Army in Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's really how Mr. Hannis put it to you and for some reason you weren't able to say yes. His question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I couldn't say yes because he -- the question he put to me is: Does it mean that you discharged both duties, and that is why I couldn't give him a straight yes answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I'm having difficulty with the concept of you holding both positions or posts but not discharging the duties of both of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, every system and military in particular has a commander, and while a commander is alive and able to exercise command, his deputy does not have the authority to command. And that is why the legislator through this organisation authorised me to be able to discharge those duties in the absence of the commander without needing any special legal act or document to authorise me to do so. I don't know whether I was clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to move next to Exhibit 3D690. This is -- this is a directive regarding the plan Grom 3, which I understand translates to Thunder 3. You've seen that document before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Until my arrival in the General Staff where I took up the post of the assistant for ground forces, and the only reason why I did that was in order to learn how the operational deployment of units was to be carried out until that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, there's a limit for how acceptable it is for you to answer questions in the way you're answering them, when clearly the simple answer is yes. You are using up a great deal of time here when there isn't an issue. You were just asked if you have seen the document before, and the answer you've given makes it clear that you have. And there was no reason for you to do other than say yes. So please do your best to answer as briefly as possible. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could go to page 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I will be guided by your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, under -- in the upper left corner under the name -- or under the heading, there is a number that appears to be handwritten in, a 2-1 and some letters in front of that that are dilated in English as DT-R. Can you tell us what DT-R stands for?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: DT stands for state secret, and R means that this is a wartime document; in other words, that it deals with combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us anything about the numbering 2-1, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the number under which it was recorded in the registry, that is DT-R, state secret wartime, and then the number, 2-1, but it seems to be typewritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're correct. I stand corrected. I think it is typewritten. Now, we had some explanation about the numbering of orders from other witnesses that indicated the first number was sometimes a subject matter number and that the second number reflected chronologically where this document appeared in the series of documents about that subject matter. Do you understand that explanation and is that your understanding of how the numbering was done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What does the number 2 refer to in this 2-1? Is that a reference to the organisation, the Supreme Command Staff -- the General Staff, or is it a reference to some subject matter? Do you know what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2 designates that it was filed under number 2-1 in the log-book, in the register book. And there could be 2-1, 2, 3, 4, 5, up to 10 documents that are related to this document, they could be filed under those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 5 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think in one of your answers the other day you indicated that the 72nd Special Forces or Special Brigade was disbanded in 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exactly date. I know that it was disbanded, but I can't recall the exact date and I can't remember whether I stated that yesterday or not, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall why it was disbanded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we may have to scroll to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S -- no, it's good where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Under item 3.1 -- 3.1 about the 3rd Army under the 1st Stage, the last sentence says: "By your request, the following units shall be resubordinated to you," and the last unit referred to is BG-3, which I understand to be Battle Group 3, Tactical Group Vihor - which is translated as Whirlwind in English - from the special units corps. Now, the units I'm familiar with all bear number designators. Was it only in the special unit that they had names like Vihor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, every unit had the number designation, had its full name, for instance, 125th Motorised Brigade or infantry brigade. This Tactical Group Whirlwind, Vihor, or Tactical Group 125-1, these are the names that were used when smaller units are formed for special tasks, and also to conceal the actual identity of the unit because everybody knew -- yeah, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask is because an issue for us in this case relates to volunteers, and some volunteer units seem to refer to themselves by names like Skorpions or Tigers, et cetera. Were you familiar with any VJ unit that went by the name Phantoms?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the Army of Yugoslavia there were no volunteer units; there were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, I want to show you Exhibit 3D696, and this is an order from General Ojdanic on behalf of the General Staff dated the 10th of March, 1999, and this is an order to the -- actually to the 2nd Army with a copy going to the 3rd Army for their information. But my question relates to item number 1 and it makes reference to the approved plan of the Yugoslav Army DT number 8-1 of 3 February. Now, the last order we looked at had a designator DT-R which you told us meant state secret and R was for Rat, I think, for war. What's the difference here, we have DT with no R, is this just a state secret but it's not war related? Is that what that means?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please be given some time to read this order in its entirety, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you need to for purposes of answering that question, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer. I can see that I was not there at the time so I couldn't give you a proper answer really.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then I'll move on to the next item.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show the witness Exhibit P1495.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Simic, this is a document from the Supreme Command Staff from the sector for operations and staff affairs dated the 24th of May, 1999, and it will be up on your screen in a minute. And this appears to be a communication from the Supreme Command Staff signed by General Ojdanic - you can see that on the second page in a minute - to the command, the commander or Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army. And it appears to be a response to some earlier communication, and you'll see in item number 1 it says: "An announcement has been prepared on the temporary postponement of the implementation of the supreme commander's decision to withdraw parts of the VJ and the MUP ..." Were you aware of that proposed decision to withdraw parts of the VJ and the MUP from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this decision, but I know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How do you know what it was all about, from meetings of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, my personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know when that decision was discussed or that proposal was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of this document have to do with the control that had been carried out earlier, and as I said the desertion for the most part from the 7th Brigade and the 354th and the 37th Motorised Brigade forced this in some way; and this in part is a response to those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Your control, though, was carried out between the 23rd and the 26th of May, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this document is dated the 24th, so it's going on at the same time, even before you've completed your control?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, we can establish a link. On the 18th, the degree of desertion from the units was at its highest. A week or two before that there was this very strong propaganda on the part of the families of the reservists, the conscripts from the Krusevac area. They threatened that they would mount protests, that they would block some roads, go on strike, and so on. That is why it is indicated here that in order to mitigate that because of the propaganda and in order to influence them, they had heard previously that the police units would be relieved over a period of two months. An order was being prepared indicating that there would be -- that the decision to rotate the police would be changed in order to help stabilise the situation and because of the families of the conscripts, because combat preparedness, combat-readiness in some of the units, I think it's the three brigades, was really at a very low level, it was really under threat, and we had to nip this in the bud.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about item number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we might have to scroll down just a little bit on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says: "The supreme commander will regulate the issue of reinforcing MUP forces in Krusevac through the minister of the interior in the Republic of Serbia." Were you aware that this was being done at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That seemed to me to suggest that Mr. Milosevic as supreme commander had some authority over the Ministry of Interior; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go next then to Exhibit P1459. General, while that's being put up on your screen I'll tell you this is a document dated the 25th of May, 1999, from General Pavkovic to the Supreme Command Staff for the Chief of Staff in person, and it has to do with the attachment of units and organs of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down so that we can get -- yes, that's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the first item I want to read -- the first part I want to read to you is item number 1: "The resubordination of the MUP forces to the forces of VJ has not been carried out in the spirit of the above order," and it's referring to the 18th of April order that you told us about before, "for several reasons, the most important among them being: a) the inherited peacetime autonomy of those units and the related conduct of their command personnel in practice and b) the order of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command was not accompanied by a corresponding order from the minister of the interior ..." And you've seen this document before today or before you came here to testify?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You indicated where this document is from, but I can't see the signature and I can't see the date. Could you please show that to me. It is very relevant to my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We've scrolled up to the top where you can see the date.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And now the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page for the general and down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now are you able to answer, General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the first time that I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall this issue being discussed in the Supreme Command Staff in late May 1999? I know on the 25th of May you were still on your control of the Pristina Corps, but after you returned was this issue discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please specify, what issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The issue of the MUP not following the spirit of the order for resubordination to the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we saw that in the control and we indicated that in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after you got back and gave your report, were there further discussions about it in the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same answer, one of the measures - I don't see it here - we proposed to the Supreme Command Staff, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, to resolve the problems together with the president of the state and all the others, all the problems that are not within the purview of General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know what measures, if any, were taken to solve this problem? Here General Pavkovic suggests that there wasn't a corresponding order from the minister of interior. Do you know whether Mr. Milosevic took any steps to have such an order go to or issue from the minister of interior about subordinating MUP units to VJ for combat operations during wartime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to save time, I will say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I hope you're doing it to save time and because that's really what happened too, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I hate to spend time, but I think it's important to know what did happen, if you can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to speak at greater length, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think I need to, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I as a subordinate do not have the right kind of insight into the work of my superiors. Secondly, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command informed us one evening that he had informed the president with all the requests that we had come up with during the control. Now, whether the president did something after that, he did not say to us, and in terms of the developments that ensued I see that nothing was done because we were not told anything. So that is why I wanted to explain this in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Can you recall for us now what General Ojdanic told you about that, what he had said to the president, Mr. Milosevic, and what Mr. Milosevic said back to him, if anything. What do you recall about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that as for all the requests that the Chief of Staff presented and that were the findings of the control, he familiarised the president with that and that he had promised to take some measures, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page and scroll to the top of the page for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 4, General. General Pavkovic is writing and says: "It has been established beyond doubt, and we have already reported on it in regular combat and other reports, that due to the non-compliance with the resubordination orders, some MUP members and to a considerable extent entire smaller units, which 'operate' independently on the ground are committing serious crimes against the Siptar civilian population in settlements or refugee shelters - murder, rape, plunder, robbery, aggravated theft -- or robbery, aggravated theft, et cetera - and then they purposefully attribute or plan to attribute those crimes to units and individuals in the VJ." Now, were you aware of that allegation as a result of your control you carried out at the Pristina Corps, were you aware of all of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I duty-bound to respond to a document I have never seen until now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you are simply being asked whether you were aware of this, that's the allegation that's contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have been made aware of part of his allegations, but they are described in our report of the control, where there is no reference to war crimes, rapes in refugees shelters and so on, and entire units at that. If you allow me, this document was sent on the 25th. We were at the command post, or rather, within the Pristina Corps, the command. The army command had its forward command post there. Why were we not informed about all of that there and then on the spot?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General Pavkovic here says we have already reported on it in regular combat and other reports, those are the reports that you would be seeing or that would filter up from General Pavkovic to the Supreme Command Staff, no? You were looking at - you, I mean the Supreme Command Staff - were looking at regular combat reports on a daily basis, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Not a single report refers to the kind of information that is contained in this document, and I've read them all from the first to the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're confident of that, that there were no mention of crimes like murder or rape, robbery, or theft being committed by MUP members or entire smaller units. There was no reference to that in any of the combat reports you read from the time that you started on April 3rd or 4th to this date, the 24th of May?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was aware of individual crimes concerning which the command took certain measures against the perpetrators; that is what I stated then too. But I do not agree that this was happening en masse by entire units. It was only individuals who were doing that. That is what the report of our control refers to, soldierly discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We may have a misunderstanding here. This report from General Pavkovic, as I read it he's talking about crimes being committed by MUP members, and your answer -- I'm not sure but your answer seemed to be -- you're talking about VJ soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about both structures from the aspect of the content of the reports that came to the staff of the Supreme Command. By this I mean our individual members too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it then you're saying that what General Pavkovic has written here and reported here is not correct, where he says: "We've already reported in regular combat and other reports ..." You're saying that didn't appear in the regular combat reports and other reports that the Supreme Command Staff got from General Pavkovic? That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in terms of these contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the earlier answer that Mr. Hannis referred to a moment ago you said: "I was aware of individual crimes concerning which the command took certain measures against the perpetrators; that is what I stated then too."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So were you aware of the command of the MUP taking measures against perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps it was a slip of the tongue. What I meant was that the Supreme Command Staff, or rather, commands at all levels in terms of their powers took measures against perpetrators of such crimes who were members of the military; as for the MUP, I do not know what kind of action they took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, that seems to give a different complexion to what you asked about. But do you want to explore it any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, General, to your knowledge did General Pavkovic or any of the subordinate VJ commanders take or attempt to take any measures against the MUP members or MUP smaller units that were allegedly committing serious crimes against the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object as to the foundation for this question. I believe, as I've been listening to this witness he has said that in fact the facts on the ground did not comport to what was in this letter. So if he's asking about what the gentleman knows or if he's asking about what's in the letter that the gentleman hasn't seen and hasn't confirmed, I'm a little bit lost by this question and where it comes out of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you look at 62, 21, you'll see that the question was related to whether there was mention of crimes being committed by MUP members, and the answer was that he was aware of individual crimes concerning which the command took certain measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He said he was aware of individual crimes by individuals not by entire units and the question Mr. Hannis now poses relates to entire units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He then in answer to me made it clear he wasn't talking about the MUP at all, and therefore it's entirely open to Mr. Hannis to find out a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In his prior testimony when I stood up for the correction in the translation, he was talking about MUP units in his report, and that's the only basis that he would have for knowledge as he's testified to here in the last exchange. And there he was very explicit not -- that it was individual persons not an entire unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's sufficient doubt in my opinion for this to be explored further. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, perhaps I should repeat the question. To your knowledge, did General Pavkovic or any of his subordinate VJ commanders take or attempt to take any measures against MUP members or against MUP smaller units that were allegedly committing these serious crimes described in this exhibit, P1459?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The MUP was not subordinated to General Pavkovic and he did the only thing he could, he reported in his combat report to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what steps -- well, maybe you answered this already. What steps did the superior command take? You told us about General Ojdanic telling the supreme commander. In your view, is that the only thing that the army could do?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing, in view of the fact that the Commander-in-Chief is his superior not the minister of the interior. His powers end by him informing the supreme commander and sending through the morning reports, reports about what is going on and reporting to the federal prime minister, to other top people in the government, the president of Serbia, the president of Montenegro, and they could see everything that was contained in the combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this as a practical matter. You're a professional soldier and I gather you have commanded units in the field, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you -- you've emphasised the importance that General Ojdanic placed on the Geneva Conventions and making sure that the subordinate units understand those obligations. In wartime when the VJ is conducting combat operations, a commander of a brigade or a battalion, he has a certain area of responsibility, does he not, in the theatre where he's operating?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And isn't it part of his responsibility as the highest-ranking soldier in that area of responsibility, isn't it his ultimate responsibility to ensure the safety of any civilians who might be in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this situation, he could not have but there is that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why do you say he could not have?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not have because not all forces were subordinated to him, those carrying out their functional tasks in that area of responsibility, starting with policemen on the beat, civil defence units who are supposed to rescue people, then civil protection units that are supposed to take care of buildings, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying that if, I don't know, Serb civilians, not in the army, not reservist, not police, Serb civilians who lived in that area of responsibility, if for revenge or some other reason started killing Albanian civilians in your area of responsibility as a VJ commander, you can't do anything - is that your position - because they're not under your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can in the sense of persuading him, telling him, not to do that or to wage war. Those are the two options.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, you strike me as the kind of individual who if you were in that situation and there were police killing civilians in your area of responsibility, you would probably wage war, wouldn't you? You would arrest those policemen, you'd stop them killing civilians, would you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I would see it personally and if these were individuals that I could cope with, by all means; but if it were my assessment that I would be on the losing end, then I would have to withdraw. Here you can see ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me go next to 4D91, 4D091. And, General, this is a document you saw before when Mr. Ackerman was talking to you. This is dated the 30th of July, 1998, from the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now this is -- item number 3 mentions that the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Pavkovic, as a member of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall attend all meetings. In the top paragraph of that order, the last two lines seem to indicate that this is being done in particularly: " ... for more efficient command of the coordinated forces and coordinated activity relating to the command in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija." So in July 1998 the VJ and the MUP were conducting joint operations in Kosovo in combatting terrorism, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you explained yesterday that even though General Pavkovic was a member of the Joint Command and attending those meetings, pursuant to this order he was supposed to talk to you, you're the army Chief of Staff referred to here, he was supposed to before going to meetings acquaint you, the Chief of Staff, with any possible request and explain to him, to you, the proposals for the engagement of forces and following your consent, I take it, then Pavkovic can go to the meeting. Is that all accurate? Did I interpret that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read this right, what it says here, and that is what we did. After the meeting he would come to me to finally verify what had already been explained at 1830.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So before these meetings he met with you and told you what the proposals were going to be that he was going to present at the Joint Command meeting, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from that point of view. He would discuss with me, well, conditionally we can call this as -- call it his preliminary thinking as to how he would act on the following day, and in this way how to make the other members of the Supreme Command aware of that. And they may have requests that may affect his preliminary thoughts. Well, then he would have to go further, but may I tell you straight away that he saw he beforehand. Later on meetings were held at the Supreme Command -- rather, usually they were around 2100 hours, it was after 1830 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that before he went to the meeting you had to give approval to the proposals he had, and that's all Mr. Hannis asked you about and now you give us a different account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that I've been telling the same story all along. At 1830 in terms of the work plan of the forward command post it is regulated that the subordinates that I was authorised to command come and report about their activities that they had during the course of the day, and then they say what they're going to do on the following day. Then I approve that decision. That is what the army commander meant, or rather, that he would come to see me beforehand, and then with that decision he goes to the joint staff, or rather, he says what it is that he's going to do, what the MUP is going to do and the other structures. And if there are important requests of theirs that would jeopardize my decision, then he is duty-bound to come back to tell me about it and to ask for subsequent approval. That is what I said yesterday and that is what I confirm today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll take that as a yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple of times, General, you're translated as having said "the Supreme Command," but I assume here you meant to say Joint Command, that's what we're talking about, the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a slip of the tongue. We are talking about the Joint Command. I don't think, actually, there was a slip of the tongue on my part. It must have been the interpretation. It was meetings of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thought that's what you meant. I just wanted to be sure we had it down correctly. Item number 3 then goes on to say: "After the meeting," of the Joint Command I assume, "the commander of the Pristina Corps shall report to the army Chief of Staff on the proposals," and here it's translated as, "on the proposals which have been accepted." And in this context I take that to mean Pavkovic comes back to you and tells you about the proposals which have been accepted by the Joint Command because he's coming back to you after the meeting; is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not properly understood or the interpretation was not good. My decision with which General Pavkovic went to the meeting of the Joint Command is unequivocal and clear. At the meetings of the Joint Command, both sides say what it is that they're going to do on the following day. He says what kind of decision he approved and the MUP says what they are going to do. They coordinate activity in terms of their specific activity. If these requests of the MUP for support that should come from the military units significantly jeopardize the implementation of tasks from my decision that I had approved, then he goes back and asks for subsequent approval or disapproval of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's another yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when -- when was the first time you heard of this Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous talks I said that I heard -- first heard of the staff of the overall forces of the MUP from an order issued by an army commander, and that from his oral order to attend meetings I found out that this was a staff of the MUP and -- and when I went and organised work at the command post I found out that -- well, he was ordering this over here, that Pavkovic attend meetings of the Joint Command. That is when I first found out about this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You first found out about it when General Samardzic issued this order that Pavkovic should go to these meetings of the Joint Command; is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you found out that Pavkovic was a member and that Samardzic was ordering that he go to those meetings, did you make any inquiries to find out what the Joint Command was exactly and who was on it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask because I thought it was not necessary, and I realised what the methodology was while I was a member of this MUP staff in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you not know in the summer of 1998 who the members of the Joint Command were, other than General Pavkovic? Did you at least know that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never attended those meetings and I never knew who was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You weren't the least bit curious and you didn't ask General Pavkovic about who's at the meetings and who's in charge, any of that stuff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it did not affect my decision at all. My decision was the law. It was respected, and from that point of view there was no need for me to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you weren't curious about why General Samardzic had ordered you to let Pavkovic go to these meetings of some body called Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ordered me because while I was at the forward command post he had resubordinated the Pristina Corps to me, and then he conveyed his authority to me that I make the decision. And that is why this order is the way that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, it just seems to me that you as a soldier and a commander, the word "command" has special significance beyond what it might have for me as a civilian. And your subordinate, General Pavkovic, is going to meetings of a Joint Command and you weren't the least bit curious about who was in this Joint Command? I know that's what you said before, I just want to confirm, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I don't understand. How many times is he supposed to answer this question in order to exhaust Tom Hannis's curiosity. He's answered it several times, and since you're -- since you're allowing him to examine far longer than what the chief took, then why do this so many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think you're right about the first point, Mr. Hannis will be satisfied with the answer he got. Your second point depends on how you define the chief. If you take the examination by Mr. Visnjic plus Mr. Ackerman plus Mr. Bakrac, then Mr. Hannis has not exhausted that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the way, let me be quite precise. I don't think that he is wasting time. I think he's doing his job very well because there are different ways of spending time in Serbian, one can imply that you're wasting time and the other one that you're using time properly. Well, that is what I meant, so I don't want to be misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were not misunderstood, Mr. Fila, but if he had been going beyond the length of what one might fairly regard as examination-in-chief on behalf of any of the accused plus the half-hour that I think he's entitled to for the statement, then we would be drawing that to his attention. He's not got all that long to go, but no doubt he's aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you know where the Joint Command meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm. If you're happy with a rough answer, I think at the MUP building, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your forward command post at this time was in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the 15th Armoured Brigade barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to now go to Exhibit P1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a document dated the 22nd of March, 1999, and it's coming from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. There's no signature, there's just a typed block at the end that says "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." We'll look at that last page in a minute. This purports to be an order to rout and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the Malo Kosovo area. Have you seen this document before you came to testify?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I was being proofed, this took place before I was at the Supreme Command Staff. Therefore, I do not believe that I'm competent to comment on anything like this because at the time I was not responsible for this sort of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at the last page of the document in both languages, I think that's page 5 of the B/C/S and 8 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this order has many of the characteristics of what we've seen in other regular VJ orders in terms of deploying units and giving them directions. I just want to bring to your attention the last sentence before the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. It says: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command and direct all forces during combat operations from the Pristina area." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you've commented on that yesterday, but as I read that, that seems like it contemplates VJ forces and MUP forces being commanded by this Joint Command, whoever that is, isn't that how that reads?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, if I may, that I'm not willing to comment on this because I wasn't there then. But if I must, I discussed yesterday in the function of the type of command post who was there and what their names were, and then I linked the so-called Joint Command which was in a particular place but the chains of command went down the established chain. Everybody exercised command over those subordinate to them, and that was the function that I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go back to page 1 of this document just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I want you to look at the number on this order in the upper left corner. And you see that strictly confidential number 455-56?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next exhibit, P1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a document entitled: "Amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP in breaking up and destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Malo Kosovo." And in the upper left-hand corner you'll see a number that is 455-56/1. Now, wouldn't that suggest that this document relates to the earlier one? It's got the same number followed by a slash 1.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not familiar with the numbering system in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I explained by use the example of that directive. When you asked me about 2/1 what it meant, the slash 1 bit, so that was the same system that was applied here, except here they used three digits, so to speak, in order to link this up with the other document. I apologise, I'm not sure if I'm being too extensive, because if that was active, only that number, and then that number had another number added to it just to link that document up to it and the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see the title of this document is: "Amendment to the decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of both the English and the B/C/S and scroll to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see this amendment comes from General Lazarevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it does appear to be authentic with a signature and a stamp and delivery information at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So to me, General, that looks like General Lazarevic is making an amendment to the order that came from the Joint Command, but I can tell you, and my colleagues will point out if I'm wrong, there's nothing in the amendment that changes what was in 455-56, Exhibit P1966, the portion about the Joint Command commanding the forces engaged in the operations. So it appears that General Lazarevic is accepting the order issued by the Joint Command, with the exception of the amendments he made here. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, you're taking me back to something and expecting me to explain it when I, in fact, wasn't the responsible person for that. The first document that you showed me, I didn't see any signature by that Joint Command, I didn't see who the commander was issuing the order in order to be able to answer this question for you and you're asking me if Lazarevic had the right to mention this or not. If I could see who the commander was of that Joint Command, then I could answer whether he had the right to amend this or not. Things being what they are, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you another one from a time when you were in the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exhibit P1878, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I will tell you this is a document dated the 15th of April, 1999, it has a number of 455-148, and it's from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, again with that typewritten signature block. And you'll see this is titled: "Order to break-up and destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the Rugovo sector."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could just go to the page 5 of the English and of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again you'll see that the last line before the signature block says: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command all forces from the Pristina sector during the conduct of combat operations." Now, unless you think I'm just being unnecessarily redundant, I want to show you Exhibit P1487. And while we're waiting for that to come up, General, I will remind you and the Judges that we were just looking at P1878 which is dated the 15th of April, 1999, and its number was 455-148. And the one I want you to look at now, General, is our Exhibit P1487. It's a document dated the 17th of April, 1999, from the Supreme Command Staff, the staff operations department, operations and administration. And if we could look at that first half of that document. You'll see this is to the 3rd Army command, to the commander personally, and it says: "Link: Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order, strictly confidential number 455-148 of 15 April 1999." That's the document we just looked at that said the combat operations should be commanded by the Joint Command, and this is from General Ojdanic. I don't know if we need to go to the bottom of the page for you to see his signature or if we have to go to the next page -- there. You can see that, that's from General Ojdanic, correct? And this is entitled: "Suggestions." Are you familiar with a military document like "suggestions"? I'm used to seeing "directive" and "order" and "decision," but is "suggestions" a common sort of document used in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suggestions come from a lower-ranking level and go up to a higher-ranking level, but not the other way around. But this is not something that is illegal. These are exceptions basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand your answer correctly then, this -- these suggestions from General Ojdanic in the Supreme Command Staff of the VJ, you say suggestions coming from -- come from a lower-ranking level, I understand you to say then that the Supreme Command Staff is lower ranking than the Joint Command, because they're making suggestions to General Pavkovic, a subordinate of the Supreme Command Staff about what he might do in relation to that Joint Command order of 15 April?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this question for you. I can't keep it down to a yes or no. I would need to elaborate. You asked me when I heard about the terms "Joint Command Staff" and that sort of thing and I told you that, didn't I, and now I'm putting it to you, you didn't ask me that. I do not permit this -- or rather, do you permit me to elaborate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think you've answered the question as best you can. I don't want you to elaborate, but if the Judges do or Mr. Visnjic does, they'll have a chance to let you talk about it later. I'd like to move on to another question now. And at least you would agree that document shows that the Supreme Command Staff is aware of the existence of a body called the Joint Command and aware of the fact that they've issued at least one order with a particular number on the 15th of April, 1999. You must agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary and to a deepest regret, I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess I'm having a hard time understanding that. How can you say that document doesn't show that the Supreme Command Staff is aware that there's a body called the Joint Command and that they issued an order with a particular number on the 15th of April, 1999, it says it right in the document, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff can only know what it receives in the form of an operations combat report and nothing beyond that. You didn't ask - and I've never seen this document before or I had never seen this document before, before I was being proofed for these proceedings, and that is why I required a while ago a lengthier explanation which again you failed to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, your job is to answer the questions, not to set the agenda. And what you've been asked just now is whether this document indicates, first of all, that the Supreme Command Staff were aware of the existence of a body called the Joint Command. Do you agree that that's what it indicates or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I can't put the second point to you in these circumstances. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a couple questions, General, related to your statement which is Exhibit 3D1089. I'm sorry, I guess I only have one question, you answered one before. You explained how documents at the Supreme Command Staff were handled, how orders were drafted, and in paragraph 29 you said: "Having completed a draft document, the person responsible takes it to be signed," in the case by the Chief of the General Staff. "Then it is taken to the office where it is recorded in the register under a specific number, a stamp with number and date, and the signature of the person issuing the order is certified with a round stamp." And where are -- where are the registers kept at the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the office of the Supreme Command Staff, or rather, in the register, to put it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And do you know how the numbers were assigned to those orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's the so-called register, it's a book. This is entered into the main register under that number, and then it has certain boxes, ordinal numbers attaching to certain documents. And now the main document that you asked me about, 2/1, there's the principal number and there is the possibility of more secondary numbers. This is kept by a person who is in charge of doing just that, he's in charge of keeping the register, the register keeper. He's in an office and normally there are another two or three persons there who deal with the stamps, and these are the only people who are authorised to use certain kinds of stamps to accompany certain signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me jump back to an earlier time-period. In the summer of 1998 when you were Chief of Staff for the 3rd Army, were you aware that General Perisic had a disagreement with Mr. Milosevic about how the army was being used in Kosovo? Were you aware of that dispute?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Explicitly, no; implicitly, yes. I myself felt the consequences of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain or elaborate a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was usual at meetings that took place at President Milosevic's for there to the Pristina Corps commander and the army commander, and they went together to these meetings where certain problems were discussed. Following their arrival, certain disagreements or differences of opinion emerged between General Samardzic and the corps commander. While being proofed I saw several documents which they exchanged, they had different views on President Milosevic's decisions at that meeting, and that's why I say that I felt the consequences of these disagreements too because I myself was in situations where I had to challenge certain decisions made by the corps commander because I had been ordered to do just that by my commander. General Pavkovic said that at the meeting, at the president's, the decision that had been taken was a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be a translation problem, but that's not the answer to the question which you did ask which was about Perisic. And there's been no reference in the answer to General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you misunderstand the question, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not contact General Perisic. I cannot simply jump the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, but the question was: Were you aware that General Perisic had a disagreement with Milosevic about how the army was being used in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's easy, this game, isn't it when you listen carefully to the question and try to give a short answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you know about that dispute between Perisic and Milosevic in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic was adamant that the army should not be used to crush the terrorist army of Kosovo without previously declaring a state of emergency and imminent threat of war. President Milosevic, for reasons known to him, did not wish to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Were you aware that in late July 1998 General Perisic apparently was upset with General Samardzic about some use of General Samardzic's forces in Kosovo? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P922. And, General, this is a -- these are the minutes of a meeting of the VJ collegium on the 20th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of the English and I think it's page -- I'm sorry. Page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we'll have a break here in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the B/C/S I need the middle paragraph, the last six or seven lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'm going to be reading the English and you tell me if this is correct. This is General Perisic speaking. He says: "I would kindly ask those of you who are to give proposals for further use of the army, make sure to give me your suggestions to fight this. I issued an order - I ban the use of the army except in the defence of the border area, where it is to act in full compliance with combat, to protect military facilities, and defend army personnel. In any other situation, the decision to use it must be made here - and let them propose why and how. Just refer to that order, why was the army used despite my order, specifically. Find out about the circumstances under which that happened, who violated the order and the proposal, the deadline, and we'll see what to do." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the paragraph immediately above that you'll see there -- about six lines up there was a reference, talking about a problem of the MUP at Orahovac: "... and Samardzic, he used a combat group, the closest to take action towards Orahovac, that's why I'm against it, not because we want the MUP people to get killed, they are Serbs ..." And then I skip a bit: "But if the army is used like that, in an unplanned manner, primarily, it slowly draws in. There's no chance that a unit, whichever unit goes down there, to the border, you can never again and then pull out another brigade, no chance." Do you recall this incident and whether there was any communication between Samardzic and Perisic about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a collegium of the General Staff. I suppose that Samardzic, too, was at the meeting but I can only assume this. I don't know this for a fact, and that's why I said that the conflict, what you refer to as a conflict, was not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one more before the break, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 22 of the English and it would be page 21 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is still the same meeting and this is still General Perisic talking. And -- I'm sorry -- yes. The B/C/S, if we could go to the middle of the page and I'm going to read from the middle of that middle paragraph, General. It says: "Paja" which I guess is somebody's name or nickname. "Paja put in responsibility of the 3rd Army commander when units of his army were used without my order." As the Chief of Staff for General Samardzic at that time, did you see any written communication from General Perisic about that complaint from General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Then I don't see any reason for any objections to be raised or any complaints to be brought to me about the commander who is exercising command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just didn't know the relationship between you and General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a good time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Simic, we will have to break now for half an hour. We will be back at 4.00. Meanwhile, could you again please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I won't be much longer with you. Mr. Ackerman asked you some questions about your opinion of General Pavkovic, and you told us he was a very capable, educated, and responsible officer. And then you indicated to us that his final assessment by General Samardzic was the rank of exceptional, which I take is the high mark. I have a question for you about evaluations or assessments in the VJ. Do you have any idea what -- well, first of all, can you tell us what were the rankings, how many categories were there? I'm in a system where we had five from outstanding, excellent, fully satisfactory, below average, and not meeting standards. Did you have some kind of equivalent system in the army or were you ranked from 1 to 10? How was that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two types of grade, one was favourable or unfavourable. Unfavourable means what it says, unfavourable. Favourable could mean good, very good, or excellent. Favourable, excellent, that is the wording used if someone excels in their professional capacity and we saw that yesterday in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've been in some systems where there were set rules by personnel that said a certain percentage of people had to be rated in this slot, in the medium slot, in the high slot, but I've also been in agencies where there was no rule. And sometimes over the years it developed that 90 per cent of the people were rated as excellent. Do you -- can you tell us what it was like in the VJ? Do you have any idea of, say, out of 100 officers what percentage of those 100 generals or 100 colonels and generals would be rated exceptional or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer specifically, explicitly there is no rule. It is normal and usual in a unit that not everyone can get the highest grade, excellent, because then one could no longer motivate anyone to strive for that sort of grade. But I can't say that 10 per cent of those rated as excellent are so-and-so, 30 per cent of those rated very good, I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you yourself, did you get a rating from General Samardzic before you left?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What ranking did you get?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about this. General Pavkovic, when he was appointed commander of the 3rd Army by the Supreme Defence Council in late 1998, during a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council Mr. Djukanovic, the president of Montenegro, raised an issue, he said that he had heard that there had been problems with the Pristina Corps operating outside the constitution in the orders of the Supreme Defence Council. And so he had a reservation about General Pavkovic. Had you heard anything about that in 1998 or after?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything from your boss, General Samardzic, or from General Perisic, or General Ojdanic in a way a complaint about General Pavkovic sometimes going around his direct superior and going directly to Mr. Milosevic, for example? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you or -- would you yourself or did you ever hear any of your colleagues describe General Pavkovic as being ambitious, a climber, if you will, within the hierarchy of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the nature of each soldier that they should strive to reach a position as high as possible, but I suppose that applies to your profession, too, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does, and I know some colleagues that I would describe as being more ambitious than others, and I just wondered if you had a view or had heard anyone express that perhaps General Pavkovic was more ambitious than the average?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about gradation, you could say that he was ambitious, rather ambitious even, but all within the boundaries of positive human ambition and in a bid to achieve as much as possible in his own profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Then I wanted to ask you about something that Mr. Bakrac asked you. Do you know where in Djakovica the forward command post of the Pristina Corps was located in 1998? Do you know what part of town that was in or was it outside town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the town facing the border, the barracks of the border battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Two more topics and then I'll be done. One, you were talking to Mr. Bakrac about a Joint Command post, and in your answer at page 37 yesterday, line 15, you said: "It's often the case that in a certain area where combat operations are afoot actions are being carried out by a number of different bodies that do not share a single chain of command. And in order to unify all these different units belonging to different bodies or structures -- and to bring about some degree of coordination to prevent conflict in the area, what one does is set up a joint command post." In Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, indeed that's what was happening, wasn't it, that there were joint combat operations by units belonging to two different bodies or structures in terms of chain of command, that is, the army, the VJ, and the MUP, correct? They did not share a single chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two bodies did not share a single chain of command, but you used two terms that I did not explain in that way yesterday. I'm not sure if that's what the transcript stated; if so, may that please be corrected. I talked not about a shared command post, but rather about a joint command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So wouldn't it have made sense to have a joint command post in Kosovo for the MUP and VJ when they were carrying out combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In which cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Petrovic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a misunderstanding about the term "joint" and "shared command post" and the witness is saying "joint," which is what we see on page 89, line 24. Line 90 -- or page 90, line 1, there is talk of a joint command post. To make matters even more complicated the interpretation the witness got was "objedinjeno komandno mesto". That's what the witness heard in Serbian and his answer was in relation to "objedinjeno komandno mesto" because that's what he heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm not following this. In line 24 he said that he talked not about a shared command post but rather about a joint command post and then Mr. Hannis asked him about a joint command post making sense in Kosovo. They seem to be using the same English language at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's how it struck me, what I said. If I'm mistaken, please accept my apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not clear to me, Mr. Hannis, that there is anything amiss in the interpretation here, but if you wish to clarify it further --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm comfortable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last topic, General. Mr. Bakrac asked you about Exhibit P969.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could have that on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
