utterances.text: And you told us about how in that summer of 1998 you were placed in charge of the use of heavy weapons, large-calibre weapons, that you were designated to be the person in charge of deciding when and whether those would be allowed to be used. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you used the term "heavy weapons," and the term we use is large-calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you use that term "large-calibre," can you tell us specifically how big a calibre and what kind of weapons we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean artillery weapons, 105-millimetre and up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the fact that you as Chief of Staff --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, excluding 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. And one of the reasons for that was because this was -- this was a sensitive issue at the time, was it not? The international community -- some people in the international community had been alleging that the army was inappropriately using large-calibre weapons in these operations against the terrorists; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about April or May when I was at the forward command post and I had the authority, this was in reference to weapons of a large destructive power that could cause more damage and destruction. That was what my decision-making power was. It wasn't about any foreigners being in the area or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could look at the exhibits on the screen now, this is P969, and I think Mr. Bakrac talked to you about it yesterday under order number 2. And I don't know if it's possible for me to see the English on the screen. My case manager will help me out. Okay. It says before -- number 1 says: "Before opening fire, unit commanders are to assess whether international observers are in the sector of combat disposition of Siptar terrorists; and if they are, do not open fire." Now, if you would go up two paragraphs from that and read -- I'll read the sentence there in English it says: "The delegations comprise between five to ten members who have unlimited access to villages, towns, and settlements. Siptar terrorists are taking advantage of the circumstances and are trying to provoke units of the VJ to open fire in their presence in order to show the world how much they are threatened." So, General isn't part of the reason that there was some -- this order was issued and there was some control put on who could authorise the use of those heavy weapons, it's because the VJ did not want these international observers to see you using large-calibre weapons against the terrorists; isn't that the reason?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I think you are confusing two different time-periods that you've already asked me about, and I provided answers. In May and in June I was at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, and that's when I enjoyed this particular power. What you're talking about now is a later period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in July 1998 you did not have that power?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in July 1998 when General Lazarevic issues this order, isn't one of the reasons for it being issued is because the VJ did not want the international observers to see the army using large-calibre weapons in anti-terrorist operations. Isn't that the reason for that or one of the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the simple reason that the use of a large-calibre weapon is not something that you can conceal, regardless of an international presence, the presence of diplomats or God knows who. I'm talking about the safety of those people, to keep them from being harmed, and that was the order. Let me remind you about previous documents. You saw for yourself that the corps commander ordered the same thing. If there were terrorists among civilians, for example, that there should be no firing, that buildings should not be fired at if the assessment is that there are still civilians in the buildings, regardless of the fact that there was firing coming from those very buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, General, but if that were the case then I don't understand why this order needs to include the language about "the Siptars are trying to take advantage of the situation and provoke units firing in their presence to show the world how much they're threatened." If all you want to do is protect foreign civilians, why don't you say: If there are foreign civilians in the area, don't fire because we don't want them to be harmed? Wouldn't that have been the plainest, most straightforward way to deal with that if that's the only reason?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this then and I think I'll be done. In answer to a question from Mr. Bakrac yesterday on this issue - and you're talking about the time-period when you were in charge of some control over large-calibre weapons, but I think the logic applies to the later period as well - you said: "The reason being I wanted to prevent the lower-ranked commanders from abusing their position, not so much that I wanted to keep them from using certain weapons inappropriate and not what the situation called for. You have a terrorist and you target them with an artillery weapon which is a commonplace example of a common mistake." And I think Judge Bonomy asked you about that. That was a mistake, wasn't it, that was an inappropriate disproportionate use of force to use an artillery weapon against a single terrorist, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I may have overreached, I vulgarized the particular example and now you're pressing me on that particular example. There were no such examples. But in certain cases in order to prevent disproportionate use of force, we restricted that. Initially this went through me, at a later stage through decisions being approved and proposals being made to the commander as to which particular piece of equipment would be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. General, thank you. I'm finished. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you sit down, Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You indicated a inquiry at least in respect of the authenticity of three of the briefing notes and you have referred to at least two of them, possibly all three in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm relying on representations I've had from Mr. Visnjic that we will have a witness later on who will explain the provenance of these, and I'm satisfied that that's probably going to pan out as he says. And then I will be satisfied with them. I think we're going to have, actually, the note-taker from which the typewritten documents were prepared. Have I stated -- may I ask if I've stated that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the position, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. May I just inform you that the full version of this document is inside the system, it's 3D1094. That is the complete document. This is alongside with other documents part and parcel of our motion number 5 to add further exhibits, and this was filed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since there is at least a question mark over these and since there will be more elaboration of their provenance, we will mark these for marked for identification, that's 3D639, 3D724, and 3D725.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That places no barrier in the way of them being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see that the entire set of briefing notes has been uploaded in e-court and it appears as 361 pages, but it does not appear that we have an English translation yet. So that's an issue that we'll continue to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we're dealing with here is a full set of documents divided by days. If Mr. Hannis looks at our individual documents, the ones that we file based on days when briefings were held, these are in actual fact the typed-up version of the handwritten set. I can name the numbers for him which number is in reference to which day to facilitate this process for him, but we can deal with that outside the courtroom. I don't think that should be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the 361 pages have been translated in individual segments?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether all the days had been translated, but certainly all up to the 10th of July. I'm not sure about later, after the 10th of July, because there's about ten days left, that leaves us with another ten days and I do have to check that. So between the 24th of March and the 10th of July, all had been translated. I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] June, June, Your Honour, the 10th of June, not July, my apologies, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you've been asked a number of questions about the Supreme Command and the Supreme Defence Council. We have seen a decision of the 23rd of March adopting rules of procedure of the Supreme Defence Council, so that's more or less at the start of the conflict with NATO. Were you aware of these rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It does say in Article 3 that: "The President shall convene the Supreme Council sessions at his own initiative at the proposal of the members of the Supreme Council or Federal Minister of Defence and Chief of General Staff. Federal Minister of Defence and Chief of General Staff or their representatives are obliged to participate at the Supreme Council sessions, otherwise the session cannot be held." Were you aware of that rule?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely familiar with the rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you have any recollection of a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council taking place after the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, do you mean 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: During the period from the 4th of April, 1999, when you were part of the Supreme Command Staff, were any generals or admirals appointed, promoted, or retired?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know about that, but I can't tell you exactly who, what rank, what duty, or if someone perhaps retired. It has been quite a long time and this time has taken its toll.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. So are you saying that you don't know if any were appointed, promoted, and retired during that period, or are you saying that there certainly were some but you can't remember who they were?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was yes, but I can't tell you about specific cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This -- these rules include Article 4 which says: "The Supreme Council shall decide on appointments, promotions, and retirements of generals and admirals with consensus pursuant to the proposal of the Chief of the General Staff." Can you recollect any meetings being held of the Supreme Defence Council after the 4th of April, 1999, to deal with the appointments, promotions, and retirements that you do remember were made?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that the rules of procedure are totally unknown to me. I know that some people were forced into -- made to retire, but whether the Supreme Defence Council actually met or not, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was your answer about appointments, promotions, and retirements confined to people who were made to retire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was talking also about people who were promoted to a higher rank; I was among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you referring in that connection to your promotion to take up the post on the 4th of April or to a different promotion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that I was promoted not to take up that post because I already had the appropriate rank to hold that post. But I said that I was promoted in that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On which date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't really give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it after the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it before the end of June?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bakrac, you wish to cross-examine further, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have just three or four -- two or three questions that are related to some of the documents exhibited by the Prosecution and they also stem from the cross-examination where I believe there may have been some prejudice to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on then, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be expeditious and to be able to complete this in five to ten minutes, could we please have Prosecution Exhibit P1966 up on e-court. Mr. Simic, while we're waiting for this document to come up on the screen, in order to be completely fair towards you, I would like you to look at this document in some detail, not just the first page and the last page as the Prosecutor asked you to look at it, and then I will be asking you some questions about it. I don't have it on my screen, I don't know if you do.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you see it now, General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- now it's gone. Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Try and look as closely as possible. I would now like to ask you, in your capacity of a high-ranking officer with many years of service, could you please just skim through this document, go through paragraph 1, and in particular paragraph 2 tasks, and then we will move on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask for the page to be scrolled up so that we can actually see paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, could we move on to the next page to look at paragraphs 3, 4, and 5, could you just skim through them as quickly as possible so as to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you pay particular attention to paragraph 5, tasks of units.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General -- and could you please look at the next page because the tasks ton on to that page so that we are sure that you really have read everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So can we comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, my question to you is: You were shown this order that is entitled or has a heading: "The Joint Command for KiM." Once you looked at those tasks, what structures, what units are referred to in this order or ...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 5.5.1, 2, and so on refers to the units that are subordinate to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So we're talking about military units. Those tasks pertain only to military units, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if this -- I'm sorry. If this now had been an order issued by some kind of a Joint Command, should there not be some tasks for MUP, and we can see here that we're talking about offering support to MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The superior commander in paragraph 5 issues orders to every unit within the chain of command subordinate to him in the chain of command, and here we can see that he is issuing tasks to the units that belong to him, that are communicating with him, the 125th Brigade and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at paragraph 4, that's on page 2, the last line there, could you please read it, the first sentence above paragraph 5, tasks for units.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Readiness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Readiness for the routing and destruction of the Siptar terrorist forces at hour, at date ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: There is no time or no date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is no time or no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How would you then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How would you then interpret this order that does not have any indication of time, date, or it is not signed at all, but here there's no time or date for the readiness?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't interpret it in any other way but that this order was not the order for the implementation, was not actually issued. Preparations were made, tasks were issued, but what we called "CH" hour has not been defined when this action should begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, to be as fair as possible towards you, my learned colleague Mr. Hannis, inadvertently I'm sure, read to you just one part of paragraph 13, item two in this paragraph. Could you please read, slowly and carefully, the last page, paragraph 13 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the last page of this document brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first and the second item there and comment on it and that would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please read it very slowly but both items listed here because my learned colleague from the Prosecution only read the second one.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 13: "Organise coordinated action with MUP forces concerning preparations for combat operations before the start and during the combat operations." Second item or passage: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command and direct all forces during combat operations from the Pristina area."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, am I right when I say that according to this two different commands have yet to meet and organise an operation and to coordinate this operation in its course?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to what we've just read about the time for readiness which was not defined, it is to be expected that they actually expect that a meeting would be held, yet another meeting, to determine the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, now let us move on to the last passage here that was shown to you by Mr. Hannis. All forces during combat operations, am I right when I say that we're talking about the command solely during combat operations, is this what this last sentence is all about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It unequivocally talks only about the exercise of command during combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I have to say, an order is issued for the carrying out of combat operations, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If we have this wording, does it not indicate that during the combat operations there will be a joint or a combined command post of the military and the MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. That's one too far, Mr. Bakrac. Most of your questions have been unnecessary re-examination; they're simply arguments that can be advanced on the strength of what's in the document. I think there was one question that was merited in that re-examination. Now, unless you have another subject to deal with, I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have just four questions relating to the topic opened up by the Prosecution, Exhibit P1459, that was the May 25 letter from General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I'll brief. As I indicated I only have four questions, so please bear with me. I want to clear up something the Prosecution opened up and I think the easiest way to do it is have the exhibit on the screen, the second page in both copies, item number 4. This is the Pavkovic letter you stated that you had never seen before, and at the top of the Serbian it's number 4 and I think in the top of the English it is also number 4 on the second page. Thank you. Now, sir, as with regards to the wholesale and serious allegations of crimes in this paragraph alleged against the MUP and whole units of the MUP in settlements and refugee shelters, including murder, rape, plunder, such allegations were never contained in any combat reports received by you or the staff of the Supreme Command prior to that date. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that either. We've got that answer, have we not, already, quite clearly, Mr. Ivetic. So there must be something else that you're moving on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can move on, Your Honour. I thought it was quite clear too, but then with the questioning of yourselves and Mr. Hannis, it appeared to me it wasn't clear. That was the point I objected and thought it was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer is clear that he had never seen any combat report containing that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the MUP, that's the clarification I want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. If that's clear and it's clear on the record and Your Honours are representing it's clear to you, then I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the transcript at page 66, lines 2 through 8, General, the Prosecution asked you about the allegations in this letter and you said that General Ojdanic took all steps he could by reporting the things going on to the president of Yugoslavia. When you refer to General Ojdanic reporting the things going on, I presume you are referring only to those things that you and General Velickovic had in your report because those were the only things that had been reported to you and the Supreme Command Staff at that time. Am I correct in that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I don't know what document you're talking about. You're talking about figures and I don't have those figures at my disposal, so I don't know what the document that is. I don't have it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The -- it's the transcript of the -- the report that you authored I believe is 3D692, General, so that would be the report that I'm referring to and it should come up on your screen in just a second. I could specifically cite to it -- I believe you had said that with respect to the MUP there were -- there were complaints or frustration with a lack of respect for agreements and I believe individual PJP MUP committing looting. Does that refresh your recollection? I don't know exactly where in the report. I believe it's on the third page on the -- paragraph 11, I believe it was in that report. I only have the -- yes, it is, it's paragraph 11, page 4 of 6 on the English and in the B/C/S -- and now -- now can you answer my question or do you need me to repeat it, General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure thing. When you stated that General Ojdanic took all steps he could by reporting these things going on to the president of Yugoslavia, were you referring -- you were referring to those things set forth in your report authored together with General Velickovic, because that is all that was known to yourselves and the Supreme Command Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And with regards to this report, it's in the middle of the -- it's actually the third paragraph in the English -- the third subparagraph of paragraph 11 in the English, you mention that there had been reactions to the levels of the "privileged" positions of the members of the MUP. Was this a problem that the professional MUP police officers were entitled to a salary and daily subsistence allowances under law, whereas the conscripts and mobilised persons in the army were not paid. Is that the problem that is here described as a "privilege" position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This principle of replacements or rotation of units, rest, food, accommodation for units, all this irritated our personnel and had an adverse effect on their morale. And that is why there was this huge case of desertion on the 17th of July because the reservists were not -- they did not receive the benefits that they were entitled to in order to be able to support themselves. That was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave, I think we have an error in transcript on page 107, I think that the witness mentioned MUP units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: 14, of MUP units, yes, 107 page, line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think also accommodation for the MUP units is what the general said, but I think it should be cleared up either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, just to finish up on this point, am I correct that the problem wasn't that the MUP was getting paid on time and the MUP was having its supplying -- logistics handled on time, the problem was that the conscripts and foot soldiers in the army were not being paid and were not being provided for within their structure. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me this piecemeal, but if we put the contents all together you can see what this is all about. It -- the behaviour of the MUP personnel was irritating wherever they were deployed. You can see this where it says the members of the VJ are particularly irritated by the behaviour of the special police units who are not in the brigade's zone of responsibility, lack of respect for agreements, and looting. And that's not how we trained our personnel, that's not how we taught our personnel. We did not allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, I am referring to the -- I am referring to the part of that section that talks about privileges, so I'm dealing exclusively with privileges at this point in time. These are not, in fact, privileges. These were regular parts of employment in the MUP, and the army had similar privileges, just that the army was unable to provide those benefits, I should say, they're benefits rather than privileges, to its members. Is that correct? This was not a malfeasance on the part of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're partially right with your question, but if you allow me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, if you allow me to elaborate a little bit. This is what hurt the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. He was unable to pay his personnel what they were entitled to, and you had these people who left their families, their jobs, and yet you have this other person who serves -- who is engaged in combat operations for one month and then is replaced, and our conscripts could not leave the ranks until the end of the war. And this is what rankled. I tried to present that but I was interrupted often. This is when General Ojdanic raised the issue, to propose to the supreme commander to put together persons at the highest levels of responsibility and that they should try and solve those problems, lest there should be more serious consequences. This is not what happened and then we had those desertions on the 18th and the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Again error in transcript, line 7, we miss word MUP, and in line 8, I found in the transcript word "conscript" but I think witness said "member," "pripadnik". Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I apologise, but during the war, after mobilisation, the term "recruit" and "reservists" are not used. The only term that is used is soldier, member of the Army of Yugoslavia. Even volunteers when they joined the army are regulated by all the laws of the Army of Yugoslavia and are considered to be its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that your report relates to the position of anyone who might be described as a soldier, member of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time when we had the state of war, every person in any unit, regardless of their status as a reservist or a soldier doing the national service, they all had the same rights and they were all members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your time. I hope that these are the last questions that I have for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we're drawing closer to the end of this exercise. Just a couple of questions for you, sir, more in the way of you helping me enlighten Mr. Ivetic about some documents that he asked you questions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 3D670 brought up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if you remember, Mr. Ivetic asked you a lot of questions about the order on the resubordination which you said was signed by President Milosevic, and then among other things there was a question raised about where this order was, whether you have ever seen it or not, what archives specifically, and so on and so forth. Could you please look at 3D670.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is not the order that I was asking about. I was asking about the one he testified to relating -- that said that was the MUP was resubordinated to the Pristina Corps, as identified in paragraph, I believe it was 19 of his statement. This one I am aware of; the other one I was not and that was what I was asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that help you, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour. It's what Mr. Ivetic asked. I will now be showing that document, the order of President Milosevic. We have the document before us, it has the file number and everything else. I hope that this under the condition obviously that the witness recognises the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're now dealing with 3D670 in respect of something Mr. Ivetic asked about 3D692; have I got the picture correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think he's referring to my questioning of the witness yesterday, Your Honour, when I asked about the order that was referenced at paragraph 19 of his written statement and where that was located, the order on resubordination of the MUP units to the PRK, as is in his -- in that paragraph of his statement. So it's not related to the cross that I did today as of yet, it's related to the cross that I did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand. But the first thing that you asked about yesterday was 3D692, and that's what you've just told us is the order you were concerned -- or the document you were concerned about, not 3D670.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I'm asking Mr. Visnjic just to indicate if the two are related to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't know what you're doing so just please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is about Mr. Ivetic's question in relation to paragraph 19 of the witness's statement, where the witness states that the order on the resubordination of the units was issued and so on and so forth, and then

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC ASKED HIM
utterances.text: "Did you personally have an opportunity to see this order in writing that was issued by the president of Yugoslavia on the resubordination of the MUP in this way?" And the witness's answer was: "Yes." And then there was a series of questions that followed by Mr. Ivetic about that document. All I'm trying to ask the witness now is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, is this the document you had in mind when answering Mr. Ivetic's questions about the president's order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the very same document and the substance reflects what I say in paragraph 19 of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [In English] I said we have two options to stop or to proceed, it depends on you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's always a good idea to get the formalities resolved so that we have a nice clean start on Monday on the essence of the witness's evidence. It usually takes a little while to break them in. We just need a name for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is General Spasoje Smiljanic. I hope they can use this much information to track down the right witness in the corridors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document you've just been given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of General Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know you spent the entire day waiting, but here we go, we have 20 minutes left and then we'll start and then continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: I have not been let down by my patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you state your name for the record, General.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm Spasoje Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What's your profession, sir?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm retired now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was your rank at retirement?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: Colonel-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you briefly take us through your military career and the duties and posts which you held?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: Of course I completed the military air force academy back in 1967 and I became an officer, second lieutenant, a pilot, in the ranks of the JNA. Over the further course of my career as an officer, I held a number of posts and I will point out those of particular importance to the army as a whole, the VJ eventually. I was chief of the first administration, I was commander of the air force and the air defence, and those were the two key positions that I held in my career. I did hold a number of other posts in the Yugoslav People's Army and later the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The two positions that you mentioned, chief of the first administration and commander of the air force and air defence, these were in actual fact positions that you held in 1998 and 1999; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1998 I was chief of the first administration and that had been since 1996. I remained in that post between 1996 and 1999. It was early in 1999 that I took up my duties as commander of the air force and the air defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say chief of the first administration, General, can you please explain briefly to the Chamber what this means, the first administration, and part of which body is it, which larger body?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: The first administration is an organic unit, an organic part of this sector for operations and staff affairs, which is attached to the army's General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your capacity as chief of the first administration, did you have the right or the responsibility to attend collegium meetings called by Chief of the General Staff on a weekly basis?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: No, until General Ojdanic was appointed Chief of the General Staff the chief of the first administration was not a member of the General Staff's collegium, but I did on an occasional basis attend these meetings even before General Ojdanic's time, especially in situations where the chief of the sector for operations and staff affairs for one reason or another was unable to attend these collegium meetings at the General Staff. On such occasions, I would stand in for him, I would stand in, as I said, at some of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to 3D1074, it's a Defence exhibit, the collegium meeting dated the 26th of September, 1997, the B/C/S page is 10. Page 2 in the English, paragraph 3, and all the way up to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me take you back to that time, I'm talking about September 1997. At this collegium meeting the situation in Kosovo and Metohija was discussed. Why was this particular time-period important? What developments were particularly important in Kosovo and Metohija at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: At this point in time or the period which followed, there were demonstrations in the offing, rallies by students and their parents in Kosovo and Metohija, the reason for this being the implementation of the agreement to commence the academic year, to resume the education of Albanian pupils and students.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly what was discussed at this collegium meeting. You as the General Staff, what did you discuss at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: The General Staff was reviewing the situation. We were trying to see what could possibly be the consequence of those demonstrations and rallies, would they be peaceful rallies, would they cause destruction, would they attack the army, would there be any interethnic strife as a result of these rallies, would this lead to clashes, would it not be the case that from Albania, which at the time was in a state of disarray, both in military terms and as a country, it was disintegrating. So these were all the factors that the General Staff analysed in order to be able to take measures to forestall if possible any destructive consequences that might follow these rallies, if indeed these rallies were to prove destructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now zoom in on the bottom half of the B/C/S page that we have on our screens right now. The English reference is -- well, the next page. Upper half of the page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what we see before us is General Ojdanic's contribution. Could you please focus closely on the last three paragraphs of his contribution. Let me first draw your attention to this -- rather, I'll read it for you. He says: "In addition to what I have said, I believe that the order should strictly prohibit any actions and conduct of VJ commands and units exceeding the constitutional role and tasks of the VJ and which would irritate our public and particularly the international public." General, you were at that meeting. You know what the discussion was about. How did you interpret this contribution by General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It's true that I was at the meeting, the meeting was chaired by the then-Chief of the General Staff, Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic. A comprehensive analysis was presented by General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, and General Ojdanic followed up in his professional capacity as deputy Chief of the General Staff, so he started making proposals and the proposal you've just read up was one of those. General Ojdanic is here explicitly advocating the following approach: The army should act in keeping with the constitution, the army must not do anything outside its role under the constitution. Not a single task may be performed that would lead to irritation among the population of Kosovo and Metohija, and particularly no irritation to the international public. Therefore, my interpretation of this is an attempt to peacefully approach this problem and peacefully resolve the problem that might occur during those rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about this other sentence: "We should request and emphasise this in the order that the principle of proposing and approving the decision on the use of the VJ forces must strictly be observed." I assume that the VJ at the time was involved in its regular activities as well, drills, manoeuvres, supplies, that sort of thing. How do you see this order within the context of the VJ's regular activities throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, the army is always busy doing something, performing some tasks, training, taking care of its supplies, that sort of thing. General Ojdanic at this collegium meeting requested that all movements by units be abandoned in Kosovo and Metohija precisely because of this, what we've been talking about, in order to not cause any irritation. Apart from such things as medical services, food supplies, or other extraordinary circumstances that might arise in which units might have to get involved and take to the road, as it were. What is here underlined as a request to strictly abide by the principles and proposals made on how the army units should be used, well, this is a principle that we call the principle of subordination and this is something that General Ojdanic remained adamant about throughout his time as deputy and especially in his capacity as Chief of the General Staff. The principle of subordination states in no uncertain terms that a commander shall use his unit, he shall make decisions on the use of his unit once he is in the possession of decisions and appropriate authorisation from his superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about the subordinate principle and the relations between a superior and a subordinate, can you please explain the following sentence: "I'm in favour -- I support the belief that every level of command should be responsible for the implementation of tasks stemming from their rank and the posts they're occupying. If anybody from the General Staff were to jump in and assume a job that was the responsibility of a lower level of command, it would mean interfering in other people's business and assuming responsibility on behalf of another person."

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You think that needs explanation, do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it does, perhaps the man who uttered it should explain it, but it's very difficult to see what particular value there is, Mr. Visnjic, in going through these documents and having this witness read out or be referred to what we can read ourselves and which could have been dealt with in writing without this -- it's much more important to get a witness to speak personally about things he has personal knowledge of rather than what we're hearing here. And this has been a feature of your presentation so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue or should I stop now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you can continue, but I'm hoping you'll pay attention to what I'm saying for next week's presentation. But please continue for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right, General. Let's skip this comment then. Do you remember or perhaps do you know this based on documents, how did General Perisic see these proposals made by General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: Indeed, General Perisic accepted these proposals by General Ojdanic, and he also requested that these be transformed into orders and submitted to units and that they be made binding in terms of implementation, plus the General Staff had the commitment to check how this order was being implemented down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I now have an October collegium meeting, or rather, November 1998, but this is a little more comprehensive, I'm afraid. I'm afraid five minutes or four minutes just won't do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Let's open it up and see if it's really necessary to do what you propose to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 3D664, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we have before us a collegium meeting dated the 6th of November, 1998, and this is another collegium meeting that you attended. We are about to see General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic's contribution or assessment, security assessment, if you like. Let me take you back to this meeting, and if you could please tell us what the situation on the ground happened to be at the time and let me jog your mind. This was just after the signing of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English reference is page 4, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, this is early November, in Kosovo and Metohija we already see the OSCE monitors arriving. Things being what they were, the mission was on its way in and the VJ forces were pushed back into boundaries defined by the agreement. The collegium discussed what the arrival of the mission meant in actual terms and the return of the VJ forces or the sending back of the VJ forces defined by the agreement to barracks and outside Kosovo and Metohija. So that's more or less what was discussed at this collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, General Dimitrijevic in his assessment on pages 4 through 6 of the English puts forward a prediction on what the KLA would do. Can you tell us what this prediction was? How did he foresee future action on the part of the KLA over the next period?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic conducts quite a comprehensive analysis here, and this is reflected in the document. And I do, as a matter of fact, remember that myself. He said that the overall situation in Kosovo was still encumbered by terrorism. That is precisely what he said. He said the terrorist forces were moving back into the area virtually enjoying protection from the OSCE. The verification mission, he said, were not doing enough to stop their return. They were still using military strongholds, they were entering these military strongholds, they were consolidating, they were collecting caches of weapons, they were getting new weapons, and based on his assessment they were preparing for large-scale operations in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if this is a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Visnjic. Thank you. Mr. Smiljanic, we have to complete our hearing today at this time, and we shall resume it on Monday at 9.00 in the morning. You require to be back here in time to resume your evidence then. Meanwhile, it is very important that you have no discussion with anyone, anyone at all, whether involved in this case or not involved in it, about the evidence in the case. You can meet with and discuss with anyone any other subject, but definitely not the evidence in the case. Would you now please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we shall see you again on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.30 p.m.,
